title: Technology in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain what technology is and how a few big inventions changed daily life.
summary: Technology is knowledge put to work on everyday jobs. Stone tools are 3.3 million years old, older than our species; wheels, printing and electric light came much later.

cards.headline: The oldest known tools are older than humans.
cards.body: About 3.3 million years ago, at a place now called Lomekwi in Kenya, someone knocked sharp flakes off stones. That was before any member of our genus, Homo, walked the Earth. Technology didn't wait for us. So what exactly is it, and how did a few inventions change an ordinary day?

mascot.line: Keep this definition close. Later levels keep coming back to it.

cards.fact: Technology is knowledge put to work on everyday jobs.
cards.context: Britannica puts it as applying scientific knowledge to the practical aims of human life. A sharpened stone counts. So does a light switch. Both take something people figured out and turn it into a job done: cutting meat, lighting a room. The knowledge keeps growing; the idea stays the same.

cards.fact: Squeeze tool history into one day, and electric light arrives under 4 seconds before midnight.
cards.context: Let the 3.3 million years since Lomekwi fill 24 hours. Our species, about 300,000 years old, turns up around 9:49 p.m. Wheels roll in about 2.5 minutes before midnight. Everything else in this chapter, starting with Volta's battery in 1800, happens in the last 6 seconds.

title: What Energy Is
objective: After this level you can explain energy as the ability to do work and name its main forms.
summary: Energy is the ability to do work. It is stored (chemical, gravitational, elastic) or working (motion, heat, light, sound, electricity), and it only ever changes form.

cards.headline: Nobody has ever made a single joule of energy.
cards.body: Not power stations, not batteries, not your breakfast. Energy can't be created. Everything that seems to make it is really changing it from one form into another. To see how, start with what energy actually is.

cards.headline: Energy is the ability to do work
cards.body: That's how scientists define it, and it comes in two big groups. Stored (potential) energy waits: chemical energy in food and batteries, gravitational energy in anything lifted high, the energy in a stretched rubber band. Working (kinetic) energy is busy: motion, heat, light, sound and electricity. A sandwich and a raised hammer have something in common. Both are jobs waiting to happen.

mascot.line: Hold on to this rule. Brakes, fridges and heat pumps all lean on it later.

cards.headline: Energy never vanishes. It changes jobs.
cards.body: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form into another. Your breakfast holds chemical energy, and your body turns it into motion when you walk or play. But even at its best, your body turns only about a quarter of that energy into motion, and most of the rest becomes heat. That's why exercise warms you up. Nothing was lost; it just changed form.

cards.fact: One joule is about the energy it takes to lift a small apple one meter.
cards.context: The joule is the standard unit of energy: the work done by a push of one newton over one meter. Lift a small apple (about 100 grams) one meter straight up, and you've spent about one joule. It's a tiny amount. Keep the apple in mind; it comes back at the end of this chapter.

title: Electricity
objective: After this level you can explain electric current as moving charges and what voltage means.
summary: Current is moving charge: electrons already in the wire drift slowly, but the push travels almost at light speed. Voltage is the energy each coulomb gets: one joule per coulomb is one volt.

cards.headline: Electrons in a wire crawl along at roughly a meter or two an hour.
cards.body: Yet flip a switch and the light comes on at once. Something about electricity is much faster than the electrons carrying it. This level untangles that puzzle: what electricity is, and what a volt actually measures.

cards.headline: Electricity is charge on the move
cards.body: Atoms hold positive protons and negative electrons. Opposite charges attract; like charges push apart. In a metal wire, when electrons all drift the same way, that's an electric current. And those electrons were in the wire all along, belonging to its own atoms. A wire isn't an empty pipe waiting to be filled. It comes already full.

cards.fact: Current counts how many electrons pass, not how fast they go.
cards.context: Current is measured in amperes. One ampere means about 6.2 billion billion electrons passing a point every second. Each one is slow, but there are so many that the flow adds up. And when you close a switch, the push reaches every electron in the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so they all start moving at once. The light doesn't wait.

cards.headline: Voltage is the push
cards.body: Voltage says how much energy each bit of charge gets. One volt means one joule for every coulomb, the charge one ampere carries in a second. An analogy helps, if you remember it's only a picture: a battery is like the pump that lifts water to the top of a water slide, so it can run back down. A 1.5-volt battery gives each coulomb 1.5 joules for the trip around.

title: Circuits
objective: After this level you can explain how a simple circuit works and what a switch does.
summary: Current flows only around a closed loop of conductors. A switch opens or closes a gap in that loop, and homes are wired in parallel so each device has its own branch.

cards.headline: Wire a kitchen as one chain, and the fridge only runs while the toaster is on.
cards.body: That would make breakfast awkward. Real kitchens aren't wired that way, and the reason comes from the same idea that makes every light switch work: electricity only flows around a complete loop.

cards.headline: A circuit is a closed loop
cards.body: Every circuit has three parts: a source of energy such as a battery, something that uses the current such as a bulb, and wires joining them. The loop has to run unbroken from one end of the battery, through the bulb, back to the other end. In a single loop, a break anywhere stops the current everywhere. Remember Level 3: the electrons are already in the wire. The loop lets them all move.

mascot.line: Closed means on, open means off. It sounds backwards at first, so say it twice.

cards.headline: A switch is a gap you control
cards.body: Metals such as copper are conductors: charge moves through them easily. Paper and plastic are insulators, and they stop the flow. A switch in the "off" position opens a gap in the loop, so no current can flow. "On" closes the gap and completes the loop. It sounds backwards, but in a circuit, closed means go.

cards.headline: Why the fridge ignores the toaster
cards.body: In a series circuit everything sits on one path, so each device must work for any of them to work. Unscrew one bulb and the others go out. Homes are wired in parallel instead: each light and appliance gets its own branch, with the same voltage across it, and draws just the current it needs. Switch off the toaster and the fridge keeps humming.

title: The Light Bulb
objective: After this level you can explain how old filament bulbs and modern LEDs make light.
summary: Incandescent bulbs heat a tungsten filament until it glows, wasting about 90% of their energy as heat. LEDs make light directly in a semiconductor and use at least 75% less energy.

cards.headline: An old-style light bulb was mostly a heater.
cards.body: Incandescent bulbs wasted about 90% of their energy as heat. Only about 10% came out as light. So how did they glow at all, and how do LEDs do the same job on far less energy?

cards.headline: Hot enough to glow
cards.body: Anything heated enough gives off light. An incandescent bulb uses that: current pushes through a thin filament that resists it, and the filament gets hot enough to glow. Modern filaments are tungsten, which has the highest melting point of the suitable materials. The glass holds a vacuum or an unreactive gas, because otherwise the hot filament would oxidize and burn away.

cards.fact: Edison didn't invent the light bulb from scratch.
cards.context: Scientists had worked on electric lamps for about 40 years, and in England Joseph Swan made a similar carbon-filament lamp in 1878. Edison's 1879 bulb, from Level 1's timeline, used a carbon filament too. Then his team kept testing materials, and a bamboo filament stretched lamp life to up to 1,200 hours. The race wasn't for the first glow. It was for a glow that lasted.

cards.headline: LEDs: light without the hot wire
cards.body: An LED (light-emitting diode) has no filament. It's made of two semiconductor materials, and when current crosses the junction between them, electrons give up energy directly as light. The material sets the color. Level 2's rule still holds: energy isn't destroyed, so less wasted as heat means more light per joule. LEDs use at least 75% less energy than incandescent bulbs and last many times longer.

title: Batteries
objective: After this level you can explain how a battery stores energy in chemicals.
summary: Volta's 1800 pile of metal discs and salty cloth was the first reliable battery. Every battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy, and dies when its reacting chemicals run out.

cards.headline: The battery began with an argument over a frog's leg.
cards.body: In 1791, Luigi Galvani saw frog leg muscles twitch when touched with two different metals. He called it "animal electricity." Alessandro Volta disagreed: he argued the current came from the two metals, and the frog was only carrying it.

cards.headline: Volta's pile: no frog required
cards.body: In 1800, Volta built a stack of alternating zinc and silver (or copper) discs, separated by cloth or paper soaked in salt water. It gave a steady, continuous current: the first reliable battery, and his side of the argument won. The volt, Level 3's unit of push, was named in his honor in 1881.

cards.headline: What's inside every battery
cards.body: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy. It has two ends, the anode and the cathode, with an electrolyte between them. Electrons leave the anode, travel around the outside circuit and arrive at the cathode, while charged particles called ions move through the electrolyte inside to balance them. Remember Level 4: nothing flows until the loop is closed. A common cell gives about 1.5 volts.

mascot.line: A dead battery isn't out of electrons. It's out of reacting chemicals.

cards.headline: "Dead" doesn't mean empty
cards.body: A flat battery hasn't run out of electrons. Level 3 showed they were in the wires all along; the battery supplies the energy. It dies when its reacting chemicals are used up. Recharging pushes current through it in reverse, running the reaction backward and storing chemical energy again. A charger is really a re-energizer.

title: Magnets and Motors
objective: After this level you can explain how magnets and electricity together make a motor spin.
summary: A current makes a magnetic field, as Ørsted saw in 1820. A motor puts a current-carrying coil between magnets and reverses its current every half turn so it keeps spinning.

cards.headline: In April 1820, a compass needle swung during a lecture.
cards.body: Hans Christian Ørsted sent a current through a wire, and a nearby magnetic needle turned to line up across it. It was clear evidence that electricity and magnetism are linked. Every electric motor you own runs on that link.

cards.headline: Current makes a magnet
cards.body: Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposite poles attract and like poles push apart, much like Level 3's charges. Ørsted's needle moved because a current makes its own magnetic field. Wind wire into a coil around an iron core and you get an electromagnet: a magnet you can switch on and off, strengthen or flip, just by changing the current.

cards.headline: How a motor keeps spinning
cards.body: Put a coil carrying current between the poles of a magnet, and magnetic pushes and pulls twist it: a turning force that spins a shaft. To keep it turning the same way, the motor reverses the current in the coil every half turn, using sliding contacts called brushes and a commutator. The push always points the same way round, so the shaft keeps going.

cards.fact: Michael Faraday built the first electric motor in 1821.
cards.context: He made a wire carrying current circle around a magnet, dipping into a bath of mercury to keep the circuit connected. Today's motors do the same basic job, turning electrical energy into motion, in fans, pumps, drills, hair dryers and electric toothbrushes. Count the ones in your home; the list gets long fast.

title: Generators
objective: After this level you can explain how spinning magnets inside coils of wire generate electricity.
summary: Faraday found in 1831 that a changing magnetic field in a coil makes a current. A generator is a motor run backwards: turbines spin a magnet inside coils to make most of the world's electricity.

cards.headline: Run a motor backwards and it makes electricity.
cards.body: Level 7 turned current into motion. Now force the shaft to turn instead, so the coil spins between the magnets, and current comes out. The same machine can work either way, and spinning generators make most of the world's electricity.

cards.headline: Faraday's discovery: change makes current
cards.body: In 1831, Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet inside a coil of wire makes a current flow in the wire. The key word is moving. A magnet sitting still inside a coil does nothing. What counts is a changing magnetic field, and the faster it changes, the bigger the voltage. This is called electromagnetic induction.

cards.headline: Inside a power-station generator
cards.body: A big generator has fixed coils of wire, the stator, around a spinning electromagnet, the rotor. Turn the rotor and current flows in the coils. Something has to do the turning: steam, falling water, wind or burning gas drives a turbine, and the turbine spins the rotor. Solar panels are the big exception: they turn sunlight into electricity directly, with nothing spinning.

cards.fact: A motor and a generator are the same machine, facing opposite ways.
cards.context: A motor turns electrical energy into motion. A generator turns motion into electrical energy. Level 2's rule explains why a generator never gives something for nothing: energy can't be created, so every joule of electricity it makes started as the energy of whatever spun it.

title: Edison, Tesla and AC
objective: After this level you can explain alternating current and why it won out over direct current.
summary: Edison's 1882 station sent direct current a short way. Alternating current won because transformers can raise its voltage for long-distance lines and lower it again for homes.

cards.headline: In 1882, Edison's first power station served a quarter of a square mile.
cards.body: His Pearl Street station in New York began supplying customers on September 4, 1882, the forerunner of every central power station since. It ran on direct current. By the late 1880s, a rival kind of current had started a war with it. Here's why the rival won.

cards.headline: DC flows one way. AC swings back and forth.
cards.body: Direct current (DC) flows steadily in one direction, like the current from a battery. Alternating current (AC) keeps reversing. On the US grid it goes through 60 complete back-and-forth cycles every second: 60 hertz. Level 8's generators make that swing naturally. A two-pole generator making 60-hertz power spins 3,600 times a minute: 60 turns a second, one cycle per turn.

cards.headline: Why AC won: the transformer
cards.body: Sending power far works best at high voltage: it's more efficient and cheaper. But homes need lower, safer voltages. A transformer changes voltage using Level 8's trick, induction, so it needs a current that keeps changing: AC. DC couldn't easily be stepped up or down, which made sending it far a problem. Tesla's AC could travel far; Edison's DC struggled to.

cards.headline: Watts: how fast energy flows
cards.body: A watt is one joule of energy every second. Remember Level 2's apple? Lifting one a meter every second takes about a watt. Watts also join Level 3's two ideas: volts times amps equals watts, because joules per coulomb times coulombs per second gives joules per second. A 60-watt bulb uses 60 joules every second it's on.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the joules. Remember: a kilowatt-hour is a thousand watts for an hour.

cards.fact: A kilowatt-hour is 3.6 million joules.
cards.context: That's 1,000 watts running for an hour (3,600 seconds), and it's the unit utilities measure and charge for. In apples, that's 3.6 million small apples, each lifted a meter. Swap an old bulb for an LED, which uses at least 75% less energy, and the same light takes a quarter or less of the kilowatt-hours.

title: The Power Grid
objective: After this level you can explain how electricity travels from a power plant to your wall socket.
summary: Transformers step power up to as much as 765,000 volts for long lines, then down to 120 or 240 volts for your home. Operators must match supply and demand every moment.

cards.headline: Most of mainland America runs on just three electric grids.
cards.body: The Eastern grid, the Western grid, and one that covers most of Texas. Each is a web of power plants and wires, and they mostly run on their own. Somewhere in yours, electricity is being made for your lamp. So how does it cross that web and come out of your wall?

cards.headline: Up, across, down
cards.body: Level 9's transformers do the heavy lifting. At the power plant, a step-up transformer raises the voltage. High-voltage transmission lines carry the power long distances. At a substation, transformers step it down, and lower-voltage distribution lines carry it along your street. One last transformer near your home steps it down again, to a voltage that's safer indoors. Up for the journey, down for the delivery.

cards.fact: The biggest US power lines carry 765,000 volts. Your home gets 120 or 240.
cards.context: US transmission lines run at 230,000 to 765,000 volts. The top voltage is more than 6,000 times what a 120-volt home circuit gets. Why go so high? For the same power, higher voltage needs less current, and less current means less energy lost in the lines on the long trip.

mascot.line: Supply must match demand every moment. Hold on to that; Level 18 builds on it.

cards.headline: The grid can't get ahead of you
cards.body: Here's the tricky part. Grid operators must call on power plants to supply just the right amount of electricity at every moment. Organizations called balancing authorities keep supply and demand precisely matched. If the two fall out of balance, local or even widespread blackouts can happen. So when millions of people switch things on, somewhere a power plant has to answer.

title: Coal and Gas Plants
objective: After this level you can explain how burning fuel boils water to spin turbines.
summary: Burning coal boils water; steam spins a turbine and generator, and two-thirds of the fuel's energy ends up as waste heat. Combined-cycle gas plants reuse hot exhaust for a second spin.

cards.headline: Most of the world's electricity comes from boiling water.
cards.body: Steam turbines make most of it, heated by coal, gas, nuclear fuel and a few other sources. A big power station is, at heart, a kettle the size of a building. This level follows the fire: how burning coal and gas becomes the electricity in your wall.

cards.headline: Fire, water, steam, spin
cards.body: In a coal plant, fuel burns in a boiler and heats water into steam. The steam pushes on blades attached to a shaft and spins the turbine. The turbine turns a generator: Level 8's spinning electromagnet inside coils of wire. Follow the energy and it's Level 2's rule at work. Chemical energy in the fuel becomes heat, heat becomes motion, and motion becomes electricity.

cards.fact: A coal plant turns only about a third of its fuel's energy into electricity.
cards.context: That was the US average in 2024. The other two-thirds ends up as waste heat. Nothing is destroyed, as Level 2 promised; it just ends up somewhere useless. It's Level 5's old light bulb problem on a giant scale: most of the energy leaves as heat.

cards.headline: Gas plants get a second spin
cards.body: A gas plant can skip the boiler. A combustion gas turbine, similar to a jet engine, burns the fuel and lets the hot gases spin its blades directly. A combined-cycle plant then catches that hot exhaust and uses it to make steam for a second turbine. Two spins from one fire. In 2024 the average US gas plant turned about 44% of its fuel's energy into electricity, against coal's 32%. In 2025 gas was the top US source, making about 41% of the country's electricity.

title: Oil
objective: After this level you can explain how oil forms, how it is drilled and what refining does.
summary: Oil formed from ancient marine life and fills tiny spaces in rock. Drake's 1859 well started the industry. Refineries sort crude by boiling point and crack it into gasoline, mostly for transport.

cards.headline: There are no underground lakes of oil.
cards.body: Oil sits in tiny spaces inside rock, a bit like water in a sponge. So how did it get into the rock, how do people get it out, and how does crude oil become the fuel in a car's tank?

cards.headline: Ancient sea life, slow-cooked
cards.body: Crude oil formed from the remains of tiny marine plants and animals, such as diatoms, that lived millions of years ago. Buried under layers of sand, silt and rock, they were turned into oil by heat and pressure. What's locked inside is Level 2's stored energy: petroleum holds chemical energy in the bonds of its molecules. A tank of gasoline is energy from an ancient sea.

cards.fact: In 1859, Edwin Drake struck oil just 69 feet down.
cards.context: His well near Titusville, Pennsylvania, was the first productive oil well in the United States, and it launched the modern petroleum industry. The job is the same today: drill down through layers of sand, silt and rock until you reach the rock that holds the oil and gas.

cards.headline: Refining: sorting crude by boiling point
cards.body: Crude oil is a mix, and a refinery sorts it. First comes distillation: the crude is heated, and in a distillation tower the lightest parts rise as vapor to the top while the heaviest settle at the bottom. Then cracking uses heat, pressure and catalysts to break heavy molecules into lighter ones, such as those in gasoline. From one 42-gallon barrel, US refineries make about 19 to 20 gallons of gasoline.

cards.fact: Oil moves the world more than it lights it.
cards.context: In 2025, petroleum products supplied about 89% of the energy used for US transportation. Yet petroleum made only about 0.7% of US electricity that year. Level 12's power plants mostly burn gas and coal; oil mostly ends up in tanks.

title: Nuclear Power
objective: After this level you can explain how splitting atoms heats water in a nuclear power plant.
summary: Neutrons split uranium-235 in a controlled chain reaction; the heat makes steam for a turbine, with no CO2 while running. Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years.

cards.headline: One uranium pellet holds about as much energy as a ton of coal.
cards.body: That's the US Department of Energy's comparison, for one small ceramic pellet. The energy comes from splitting atoms. And here's the surprise: once that energy is out, a nuclear plant uses it the same way Level 12's coal plant does.

cards.headline: Splitting atoms, on purpose
cards.body: Nuclear plants use uranium-235, whose atoms split easily. A neutron strikes a uranium atom and splits it, releasing a lot of energy as heat and radiation, plus more neutrons. Those neutrons split more atoms: a chain reaction. Reactors keep it under control with control rods, pushed in to slow the reaction and pulled out to speed it up. A fire made of atoms, with a dimmer switch.

cards.headline: Then it's a kettle again
cards.body: The uranium, made into pellets and sealed in metal fuel rods, heats water into steam. The steam spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator, just like in a coal plant. The difference is what's missing: nuclear reactors release no carbon dioxide or air pollution while they run. In 2025 they made about 18% of US electricity and about 9% of the world's.

cards.headline: Why people argue about it
cards.body: Spent fuel is highly radioactive and can stay dangerous for thousands of years. The US still has no permanent place to put it, so it waits in pools of water and dry containers. Views split sharply. The International Energy Agency says nuclear power can play a major role in cutting emissions. Greenpeace opposes new plants, calling nuclear power dangerous and expensive and pointing to waste and to the Chernobyl and Fukushima accidents.

title: Hydropower
objective: After this level you can explain how dams turn falling water into electricity.
summary: Water from a reservoir falls through a penstock to spin a turbine. More flow and a higher fall mean more power. Hydro made about 14% of the world's electricity in 2025.

cards.headline: America's first hydroelectric plant opened 26 days after Edison's.
cards.body: Level 9's Pearl Street station started on September 4, 1882. On September 30, a plant on the Fox River in Appleton, Wisconsin, began selling electricity made by moving water. People had used rivers to turn paddle wheels and grind grain for thousands of years. Now a river could light a room.

cards.headline: How a dam makes electricity
cards.body: A dam holds back a reservoir of water. Near the bottom of the dam, water enters an intake and falls through a pipe called a penstock. At the end it spins a turbine, and the turbine's shaft turns a generator. No fire, no steam: the water pushes the turbine itself. It's Level 2's gravitational energy, the energy stored in anything raised high, cashed in.

cards.fact: The more water, and the farther it falls, the more electricity.
cards.context: Engineers call the height of the fall the head. The amount of energy in moving water depends on the flow and the head, so a big river behind a tall dam is the dream setup. The biggest hydroelectric facility in the world is the Three Gorges Dam on China's Yangtze River.

cards.headline: Big for the world, smaller for the US
cards.body: Hydropower made about 14% of the world's electricity in 2025, but only about 6% of US electricity. It all depends on where the big rivers and big drops are. And remember Level 9's win for AC? In 1896, the power that lit Buffalo came from Niagara Falls.

title: Wind Power
objective: After this level you can explain how wind turbines work and where they work best.
summary: Wind turns blades and a rotor that drives a generator. Wind power rises with the cube of wind speed, so turbines go on windy plains, hilltops and water, on tall towers.

cards.headline: Double the wind speed, and you get eight times the power.
cards.body: That one rule explains where wind turbines stand and why they're so tall. First, what's going on up there when the blades turn?

cards.headline: A generator with wings
cards.body: A wind turbine's blades work like an airplane wing: moving air pushes them around. They turn a rotor, which drives a generator, either directly or through a shaft and gearbox. It all sits in a housing called the nacelle, on top of a tall tower. It's Level 8's generator again, except the wind does the spinning that steam does in Level 12's power plants.

cards.fact: The power in the wind grows with the cube of its speed.
cards.context: Double the speed and the power goes up two times two times two: eight times. That's why a site that's only a little windier can make far more electricity, and why small changes in wind speed swing a turbine's output so much.

cards.headline: Where the wind is worth it
cards.body: Good sites for big turbines average at least 13 mph of wind: smooth rounded hilltops, open plains, open water and mountain gaps that funnel the wind. Wind is also generally faster higher up, which is why the towers are so tall. In 2025, Texas, Iowa, Oklahoma, Kansas and Illinois made about 52% of US wind power. Across the country, wind made about a tenth of all electricity.

title: Solar Power
objective: After this level you can explain how solar panels turn sunlight into electricity.
summary: Sunlight knocks electrons loose in a semiconductor cell, with nothing spinning. Panels make DC, so inverters turn it into AC. In 2025 solar passed wind worldwide.

cards.headline: In 2025, solar passed wind as a source of the world's electricity.
cards.body: It was the first time, according to the International Energy Agency. And solar does it with no turbine at all. As Level 8 pointed out, nothing spins: sunlight goes in, electricity comes out. So how does a flat panel pull that off?

cards.headline: Light knocks electrons loose
cards.body: A solar cell, or photovoltaic (PV) cell, is made of a semiconductor, like Level 5's LED. When it absorbs enough sunlight, electrons are knocked loose and move toward the cell's front surface. That builds up a charge imbalance, like the two ends of a battery. Connect the cell into a circuit and current flows. An LED turns electricity into light; a solar cell runs the trick the other way.

cards.fact: Solar cells make direct current, so an inverter turns it into AC.
cards.context: Remember Level 9: the grid runs on AC, while solar cells make DC. An inverter converts one into the other. Cells are wired into weather-tight panels, and panels are grouped into arrays. Edison's DC lost the War of the Currents, but every solar cell brings it back.

cards.headline: Better every decade
cards.body: The first practical solar cell came from Bell Telephone researchers in 1954. Efficiency, the share of sunlight a panel turns into electricity, has climbed steadily: commercial panels averaged under 10% in the mid-1980s, about 15% by 2015, and the best modules now approach 25%. One thing no panel can fix is sunset, so PV systems can charge batteries to supply power when the sun isn't shining.

title: Storing Energy
objective: After this level you can explain why storing electricity is hard and how big batteries help.
summary: Storage turns electricity into another form and back, returning less than it took. Pumped storage lifts water uphill; big batteries shift midday solar into the evening.

cards.headline: US grid batteries grew about fivefold in just three years.
cards.body: At the end of 2022, big batteries on the US grid could deliver about 9 billion watts at once. By the end of 2025, about 44 billion. Why the rush? Level 11's grid has to match supply and demand every moment, and solar power has to be saved for when the sun isn't shining.

cards.headline: You can't bottle electricity
cards.body: Grid storage keeps energy as something else: water pumped uphill, chemicals in batteries, heat, compressed air or a spinning flywheel. Then it turns it back into electricity. That round trip costs something: storage always uses more electricity to charge than it gives back. And it makes no energy of its own, which is Level 2's rule again. Its job is timing: moving power from when there's plenty to when there isn't.

cards.headline: The water battery
cards.body: Pumped-storage hydropower uses spare electricity to run its turbines in reverse, pumping water up to a reservoir. When power is needed, the water flows back down through the turbines, just like Level 15's dam. America's oldest, Rocky River in Connecticut, began pumping in 1928. It's Level 2's lifted apple, with a lake instead of an apple.

cards.headline: Saving sunshine for the evening
cards.body: Big grid batteries do Level 6's job on a grand scale, storing energy as chemicals. In California, they charge on extra solar power at midday and give it back in the evening peak, from 5 to 9 p.m. Their average output in those hours rose from under 1 billion watts in 2022 to about 4.9 billion in 2025, replacing electricity from gas plants.

title: Energy and Climate
objective: After this level you can explain how the ways we make energy affect carbon emissions.
summary: CO2 traps heat, and burning fossil fuels has raised it over 50%. Per kilowatt-hour, coal emits the most, gas under half as much, and wind and nuclear far less. Groups argue over the path.

cards.headline: A coal-powered kilowatt-hour came with about 2.3 pounds of CO2.
cards.body: That was the US average for coal in 2023: Level 10's unit of energy, plus an invisible side order. Natural gas released less than half as much. Why does that gas matter, and which ways of making electricity release the least?

cards.headline: Why CO2 warms the planet
cards.body: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas: it traps heat from sunlight, warming the planet. Since industrial times began in the 18th century, the CO2 in the air has risen by more than 50%, mainly from burning coal, oil and gas. The IPCC, the UN body that assesses climate science, finds that human activity has unequivocally caused global warming: about 1.1°C in 2011–2020 compared with 1850–1900.

cards.fact: Per kilowatt-hour, coal emits more than 70 times as much as wind.
cards.context: That counts a plant's whole life, from building it to running it. In the IPCC's 2014 review, typical figures were about 820 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for coal, 490 for gas, and 12 or less for nuclear and onshore wind. Wind, solar and nuclear burn nothing; their emissions come mostly from building the plants and their supply chains.

cards.headline: Settled science, argued paths
cards.body: In the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries agreed to aim to hold warming well below 2°C. How to get there is fiercely argued. OPEC, the oil exporters' group, expects oil demand to keep growing to 2050 and stresses continued investment in oil. Greenpeace calls for a fast, fair phase-out of coal, oil and gas. The IEA sees a major role for nuclear power, which Greenpeace opposes. The physics sets the stakes; people argue over the route.

title: Levers, Wheels and Pulleys
objective: After this level you can explain how simple machines make work easier.
summary: Levers, wheels and pulleys multiply a push by trading it for distance. With 4 rope strands you pull a quarter as hard but haul 4 times the rope: no machine makes energy.

cards.headline: A story says Archimedes pulled a loaded ship ashore by hand.
cards.body: The Greek writer Plutarch tells it: the ship was full of passengers and cargo, and Archimedes drew it toward him by quietly working a system of pulleys. Nobody can check a story that old. But the trick behind it is real, and it hides inside some of the simplest tools there are. How can a small push move something huge?

cards.headline: A lever trades distance for force
cards.body: The lever is one of six classic simple machines, alongside the wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge and screw. It's a bar that turns on a pivot, the fulcrum. Its rule: force times distance from the fulcrum balances on each side. Push five times farther from the pivot than the load sits, and your push is multiplied five times. That's how a small kid on a seesaw can balance a big one: sit farther out.

cards.headline: Wheels and pulleys play the same trick
cards.body: A wheel and axle is a lever that goes round. Turn the big wheel, and the force at the small axle is multiplied by the ratio of their sizes. A pulley is a wheel carrying a rope. Run the rope round several pulleys so that 4 strands hold up the load, and the strands share the weight: you pull with about a quarter of the force. That's the kind of setup Archimedes supposedly used.

mascot.line: Machines will give you more force any day, as long as you pay in distance.

cards.fact: No machine gives you free work.
cards.context: The extra force always costs distance. With 4 strands holding the load, you have to haul in 4 meters of rope to lift it 1 meter. Force times distance, the work, comes out the same, and friction takes a little extra on top. Level 2's rule again: energy is never created, not even by Archimedes.

title: The Steam Engine
objective: After this level you can explain how a steam engine turns heat into motion.
summary: Newcomen's 1712 mine engine condensed steam so air pressure pushed its piston. Watt's separate condenser kept the cylinder hot and cut fuel costs; the watt honors him.

cards.headline: The first working steam engines had one job: draining flooded mines.
cards.body: Pumping water out of mines with horses was expensive. So in 1712, near Dudley Castle in England, an engine designed by Thomas Newcomen went to work instead. It turned the heat of burning fuel into motion, though not in the way you'd probably guess.

cards.headline: The air did the pushing
cards.body: A steam engine uses heat to do mechanical work: steam from a boiler acts on a piston in a cylinder. Newcomen's version was sneaky. Steam filled the cylinder, then a spray of cold water condensed it back into a little water, leaving a partial vacuum. With almost nothing pushing from below, the atmosphere pressed the piston down, and that stroke worked the mine pump.

cards.headline: Watt's fix: keep the cylinder hot
cards.body: Every stroke, Newcomen's cylinder was chilled by the spray and then reheated by fresh steam, burning fuel just to warm it back up. In 1765 James Watt had the idea of condensing the steam in a separate chamber, so the cylinder could stay hot. He patented it in 1769, and it cut fuel costs. Then, in 1781, he made his engine turn a shaft, so it could drive machines, not just pumps.

cards.fact: Level 10's watt is named after James Watt.
cards.context: A watt is one joule of energy every second: the unit behind Level 10's 60-watt bulb. It honors the engineer whose work made steam engines far less wasteful. So each time you read a bulb's rating, you're quietly crediting a steam engineer.

title: The Industrial Revolution
objective: After this level you can explain how steam power and factories changed the way people worked.
summary: From the mid-1700s, Britain moved spinning from homes into powered mills. Steam freed factories from riverbanks; long shifts and child labor led to the 1833 Factory Act.

cards.headline: In Richard Arkwright's first mills, the machines ran day and night.
cards.body: Two 13-hour shifts a day kept them turning. Not long before, most cotton spinning had been done at home. Arkwright moved it into huge powered mills with hundreds of workers. Multiply that change across a country and you get the Industrial Revolution.

cards.headline: From homes to factories
cards.body: Britain led the way, from the mid-1700s to about 1830, turning a farming and handicraft economy into one run by industry and machines. Machines such as the spinning jenny and the power loom let fewer hands make more cloth. In 1771 Arkwright began a mill at Cromford beside a fast river, whose water drove the machines. Inside, each worker did one small part of the job over and over: the factory system.

cards.headline: Steam sets the factories free
cards.body: A water wheel ties a mill to a good river. Remember Level 22: from 1781, Watt's engines could turn a shaft. With steam, mill owners could build where workers already lived, instead of hunting for the right stream. The Factory Act of 1833 banned under-9s from textile mills and limited 9-to-12-year-olds to 8 hours a day. Crucially, it created inspectors to enforce the rules: it was the first Factory Act with a way to make them stick.

title: The Car Engine

summary: A car engine burns fuel inside its cylinders. Intake, compression, power, exhaust: one push per cycle, and only about 12%-30% of the fuel energy moves the car.

cards.body: Most of the rest is lost in the engine, mainly as heat. That sounds wasteful, and it is, but the engine still gets the job done. Here's how it turns fuel into motion, one burst of hot gas at a time.

cards.headline: Fire inside the cylinder
cards.body: Level 22's steam engines made their steam in a separate boiler, then piped it to the piston. A car engine is an internal combustion engine: the fuel burns inside the cylinder itself. A spark plug ignites a mix of gasoline and air, and the hot, expanding gas shoves the piston. No boiler, no waiting for water to boil.

title: Electric Cars
objective: After this level you can explain how electric cars work and how they differ from gas cars.
summary: An electric car's battery-powered motor turns the wheels. Over 77% of plug energy reaches them, and regenerative braking runs the motor as a generator to recharge.

cards.headline: By 1900, about a third of the vehicles on the road were electric.
cards.body: Then cheap gasoline cars such as Ford's Model T, and an electric starter that ended hand-cranking, pushed them aside. Now they're back: in 2025, about 1 in 4 new cars sold worldwide was electric, counting plug-in hybrids (IEA). Inside, they run on ideas from Chapter 1.

cards.headline: Battery, motor, wheels
cards.body: An all-electric car has no internal combustion engine at all. A big rechargeable battery pack stores the energy, and an electric traction motor, Level 7's machine for turning electricity into motion, drives the wheels. Nothing burns, so there's no tailpipe and no exhaust. Level 24's four strokes, spark plugs and pistons simply aren't there.

cards.fact: Counting from the plug, an electric car gets over 77% of its energy to the wheels.
cards.context: A gas car gets only about 12%-30% of its fuel's energy to the wheels, as Level 24 showed. The difference is mostly heat: an engine burning fuel loses most of its energy that way, and an electric motor loses far less. Level 2's rule does the accounting: less energy lost means more of it moving you.

mascot.line: This is Level 8's idea again: run a motor backwards and it's a generator.

cards.headline: Braking that charges the battery
cards.body: Here's the clever part. When an electric car slows down, the turning wheels spin its motor, and the motor runs as a generator, just as Level 8 said a motor run backwards would. It makes electricity that goes back into the battery, and doing that work helps slow the car. This is regenerative braking: energy that braking would normally waste gets saved.

title: Friction and Brakes
objective: After this level you can explain friction and how brakes stop a moving car.
summary: Friction resists sliding and turns motion into heat. Brakes use it on purpose, and since doubling speed quadruples the energy of motion, it quadruples braking distance.

cards.headline: Double your speed, and your car needs four times as far to brake.
cards.body: Not twice as far: four times, with the same brakes pressing just as hard. The reason is energy, and the force that has to get rid of it is friction.

cards.headline: Friction: surfaces that catch
cards.body: Friction is a force that resists one surface sliding over another. Even surfaces that feel smooth are rough up close, and their bumps catch. Starting something sliding takes more force than keeping it going, which is why a heavy box suddenly lurches once it finally moves. Friction is also what lets your shoes grip the floor. Without it, every walk would be an ice rink.

cards.headline: Brakes turn motion into heat
cards.body: A disc brake is friction on purpose. Pads press against a metal disc that turns with the wheel, and the rubbing slows it. Level 2's rule decides where the car's energy of motion goes: it can't vanish, so it becomes heat in the brakes. Rub your hands together fast and you can feel the same trick, just smaller.

mascot.line: Twice the speed, four times the braking. 'A little faster' is never just a little.

cards.fact: Twice the speed means four times the energy of motion to get rid of.
cards.context: A car at 100 km/h carries four times the energy of motion it has at 50 km/h. Brakes pressing equally hard remove it at a steady rate per meter, so the braking distance quadruples too. Level 25's regenerative braking saves some of that energy as electricity; friction brakes can only turn it into heat.

title: Gears
objective: After this level you can explain how gears trade speed for force.
summary: Meshing gears can't slip, so tooth counts set speed: twice the teeth, half the speed, twice the turning force. Gears were predicting eclipses over 2,000 years ago.

cards.headline: On a steep hill, your bike's lowest gear makes you pedal more to go slower.
cards.body: Every turn of the pedals gets easier, but you cover less ground with it. That isn't a flaw; it's the deal. Gears trade speed for force, or force for speed, and here's how.

cards.headline: Teeth set the ratio
cards.body: A gear is a wheel with teeth. When two gears mesh, the teeth can't slip, so both gears pass the same number of teeth every second. Give the driven gear twice as many teeth as the one driving it, and it turns at half the speed. Count the teeth and you know the ratio.

cards.headline: Slower, but stronger
cards.body: That slower gear also turns with twice the twisting force, called torque. It's Level 21's wheel and axle again: gears multiply force by the ratio of their sizes, like levers that go round. Flip the pair, with a big gear driving a small one, and you get speed instead of force. Either way, Level 21's rule holds: no gear hands out free energy.

cards.fact: Gears were predicting eclipses over 2,000 years ago.
cards.context: In 1901, divers pulled the Antikythera mechanism from an ancient Greek shipwreck. Made around 100 BCE, it has 30 surviving bronze gears, and it predicted eclipses. The gears did it by turning at precise speed ratios, the same tooth-counting you just learned.

title: Hydraulics
objective: After this level you can explain how liquid under pressure lets a small push lift a heavy load.
summary: Pascal's principle: pressure on a trapped liquid rises equally everywhere. A piston with 10 times the area pushes 10 times as hard but moves a tenth as far. Brakes use it.

cards.headline: A small push on a trapped liquid can lift a car.
cards.body: No giant muscles required: just a liquid in a closed system, passing your push along and multiplying it. That's hydraulics, and your car relies on it every time you stop.

cards.headline: Pascal's principle
cards.body: The French scientist Blaise Pascal described a rule for liquids at rest in a closed container: press on one part, and the pressure rises by the same amount everywhere in the liquid, right out to the walls. It works because liquids can hardly be squeezed into a smaller space. Push the liquid here, and it pushes just as hard over there.

mascot.line: Level 21's deal again: more force, paid for with more distance.

cards.headline: Small piston, big piston
cards.body: Pressure is force spread over an area. Connect a small piston to one with 10 times the area: the pressure on both is the same, so the big piston pushes with 10 times the force. The catch is Level 21's rule. To raise the big piston 1 centimeter, the small one must travel 10. Force up, distance up, energy the same.

cards.fact: Your car's brakes are hydraulic.
cards.context: Press the brake pedal and your foot pushes on brake fluid. The pressure travels through the fluid to pistons at the wheels, which squeeze the brake pads from Level 26 with a much larger force. Because one fluid carries the same pressure to every brake, all four wheels brake evenly.

title: Why Bicycles Stay Up
objective: After this level you can explain what keeps a moving bicycle upright.
summary: Riders stay up by steering the wheels under a fall. A moving bike can steer itself upright; a 2011 bike with no gyroscopic effect or trail still did. It's a subtle mix.

cards.headline: The first bicycle had no pedals.
cards.body: In 1817, Karl von Drais rode his wooden two-wheeler 14 km, pushing along with his feet on the ground. It already had handlebar steering, and steering turns out to be the heart of balance. Why a bike stays up is, amazingly, still not fully worked out.

cards.headline: You balance by steering
cards.body: Think of balancing a broom upright on your hand: when it tips, you move your hand back under it. Riding works the same way. When the bike starts to lean one way, you steer that way, so the wheels roll back under your weight. You do it constantly without noticing. And that's why a stopped bike falls: with no rolling, steering can't fix anything.

cards.headline: A bike that balances itself
cards.body: Give a riderless bike a push at a decent speed and it can roll along upright, recovering from a sideways shove. As it leans, its front wheel steers into the lean all by itself. The usual explanation credited two things: the gyroscopic effect of the spinning front wheel, and trail, the way the front wheel touches the ground behind the steering axis, like a shopping-cart caster.

cards.fact: In 2011, a bike with neither effect still balanced itself.
cards.context: Kooijman and colleagues built a bike with extra wheels spinning backwards to cancel the gyroscopic effect, and a front wheel touching down ahead of the steering axis, so no trail. Rolling above about 5 mph (8 km/h), it still steered itself upright (Science, 2011). Where the bike's mass sits matters too. The honest summary: it's a mix of effects, and researchers say much is still to be learned.

title: How Planes Fly
objective: After this level you can explain lift, thrust, drag and weight.
summary: Lift balances weight and thrust balances drag. A wing turns air downward, so the air pushes it up; faster air above means lower pressure there. The equal-transit story is a myth.

cards.headline: A favorite explanation of how wings work is wrong.
cards.body: You may have heard it: air over the curved top of a wing has farther to go, so it must hurry to meet the air underneath at the back edge. NASA calls this "equal transit" theory incorrect. It also can't explain how a stunt plane flies upside down. So what really holds a plane up?

cards.headline: Four forces, two tug-of-wars
cards.body: Every plane in flight feels four forces. Weight pulls it toward the center of the Earth, and lift from the wings opposes it. Drag is the air resisting the plane's motion, and thrust from the engines overcomes it. Cruising at a steady speed and height, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag. Unbalance them and the plane accelerates toward the biggest force: it speeds up, slows down, climbs or sinks.

cards.headline: How a wing really lifts
cards.body: A wing is shaped and tilted so it turns the passing air downward. By Newton's third law, if the wing pushes air down, the air pushes the wing up. Now look at the same thing as pressure: the air speeds up over the top, and faster air has lower pressure, so the higher pressure underneath pushes up. NASA's point is that these aren't rival theories. Pressure and flow turning are two ways of describing one force: lift.

mascot.line: The 'meet up at the back' story is the one to unlearn. Wings turn air downward.

cards.fact: Air over the top of a wing reaches the back edge first.
cards.context: So the "meet up at the back" story fails its own test: the air on top doesn't wait for its partner. It also can't explain symmetric wings, flat paper airplanes, or planes flying upside down with the curved side at the bottom. What matters is the wing's angle to the oncoming air, its angle of attack. Pilots raise the nose at takeoff to get more lift, though tilt too far and the wing stalls.

title: Jet Engines
objective: After this level you can explain how jet engines push planes forward.
summary: A jet engine squeezes air, burns fuel in it and blasts it out of the back; the reaction pushes the plane forward. The turbine drives the compressor, and turbofans add a big fan.

cards.headline: The jet engine was invented twice, by two men working separately.
cards.body: Frank Whittle in Britain patented his turbojet in 1930. In Germany, Hans von Ohain designed one independently, and his engine flew first, in the He 178 on August 27, 1939. An aircraft with Whittle's engine followed on May 15, 1941. Both had found the same trick for pushing a plane.

cards.headline: Throw air back, get pushed forward
cards.body: For every action there's an equal and opposite reaction: Newton's third law. Every engine that moves a vehicle uses it. It grabs a working fluid, accelerates it backward, and the reaction pushes the engine forward. A jet's working fluid is the air around it, and it makes thrust because the gas leaves the back faster than the air came in. That push is Level 31's thrust, the force that beats drag.

cards.headline: Inside: squeeze, burn, spin, blow
cards.body: Air enters the front and meets the compressor, rows of spinning blades that raise its pressure. In the burner, fuel mixes with that air and burns. The hot gas rushes through a turbine and spins it, and a shaft carries that spin forward to drive the compressor. Then the nozzle shoots the gas out, faster than it came in. The turbine is a cousin of Level 8's: power stations spin theirs with burning gas too.

cards.fact: Airliners wrap a giant fan around the jet.
cards.context: In a turbofan, the big fan at the front sends some air into the core and pushes the rest around it, just like air through a propeller. The fan adds thrust while barely changing how much fuel the core burns, so the engine gets more push for nearly the same fuel. That's why most modern airliners use turbofans. The big round front you see from your window seat is mostly fan.

cards.headline: In 1964, Japan opened a railway for trains at 210 km/h.

cards.headline: Electric trains leave the power station at home
cards.body: An electric train picks up current from an overhead wire or a third rail beside the track. Britannica calls electric locomotives power converters rather than power generators: traction motors, the same idea as Level 7's, turn that current into turning wheels. The generator that made the electricity is somewhere else on the grid. The train just borrows its output.

cards.headline: Diesel-electric: a power station on wheels

It drives a generator, Level 8's machine that turns motion into electrical energy, and that current runs electric traction motors. So even a diesel train is driven by electric motors. It just makes its own electricity as it goes.

cards.fact: Shanghai's maglev floats about 1.3 cm above its track.
cards.context: No wheels touch the guideway at all. Magnets lift the train, and coils in the guideway, constantly changing polarity, pull it along: Level 7's attract and repel, put to work. Since January 2004, Shanghai's line has run daily passenger service at up to 430 km/h, the first high-speed maglev in commercial service. No wheels, no rolling, just a very fast hover.

title: Why Ships Float
objective: After this level you can explain buoyancy and how a steel ship floats.
summary: Water pushes up on a ship with the weight of the water it pushes aside. A steel hull full of air has an average density below water's, so it floats; the Plimsoll line shows how deep it may sit.

cards.headline: Drop a lump of clay in water and it sinks. Mold it into a boat and it floats.
cards.body: Same clay, same weight. Only the shape changed. That's the whole secret of a steel ship, built from a metal about 7.8 times as dense as water.

cards.headline: Archimedes' push
cards.body: Anything in water feels an upward push, the buoyant force, equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside. That's Archimedes' principle. A ship settles into the water until the water it has pushed aside weighs exactly as much as the ship. Load it with cargo and it sinks deeper, pushing aside more water, until the two weights match again.

cards.headline: Why steel can float
cards.body: Whether something floats depends on its average density. A solid block of steel is steel all the way through, so it sinks. A ship's hull is a steel shell around a huge space full of air, so the ship as a whole, steel plus air, averages out less dense than water. The clay boat works the same way: thin and hollow, it pushes aside more water than the lump did.

cards.fact: A mark on the hull shows how deep a ship may safely sit.
cards.context: After Samuel Plimsoll campaigned against overloaded ships, Britain's Merchant Shipping Act of 1876 fixed a loading mark on hulls: the Plimsoll line. title: Radar and Sonar
objective: After this level you can explain how radar and sonar find things by bouncing waves off them.
summary: Radar times radio echoes and sonar times sound echoes; half the round trip at the wave's speed gives the distance. Radio travels at the speed of light, sound in seawater at about 1,500 m/s.

cards.headline: In February 1935, a green spot grew on a screen in a parked van.
cards.body: Inside, Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins were watching radio waves from the BBC's Daventry transmitter bounce off a bomber about 8 miles away. The spot proved that radio echoes could reveal an aircraft. The trick was an echo, and it's the same trick ships use underwater.

cards.headline: Radar: shout, listen, time it
cards.body: Radar stands for radio detection and ranging. It sends out pulses of radio waves and listens for echoes. Distance comes from timing the round trip, out to the target and back, then halving it. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 km every second, so an echo from a plane 150 km away comes back in about a thousandth of a second.

cards.headline: Sonar: the same trick with sound
cards.body: In water, sound travels much farther than radar or light waves, so ships use sonar (sound navigation and ranging). It sends a pulse of sound into the water and times the echo. Sound crosses seawater at about 1,500 meters per second. Hear the seafloor's echo 2 seconds after the ping, and the sound has gone 3,000 meters round trip: the bottom is 1,500 meters down.

cards.fact: Radar can also tell how fast something is moving.
cards.context: A moving target shifts the frequency of the echo it sends back, and the radar reads that shift as speed and direction: the Doppler principle. That's how radar helps with air traffic control, tracks storms, and catches drivers going too fast. One echo, two answers: where it is, and how fast it's going.

title: Rockets
objective: After this level you can explain how rockets push themselves forward in the vacuum of space.
summary: A rocket pushes on its own exhaust, not on air, and carries its own oxidizer, so it works in a vacuum. Goddard flew the first liquid-fueled rocket in 1926.

cards.headline: In 1920, a newspaper said rockets could never work in space.
cards.body: The New York Times mocked rocket pioneer Robert Goddard, claiming a rocket in a vacuum would have nothing to push against. On July 17, 1969, with Apollo 11 on its way to the Moon, the paper printed a correction. Who was right says a lot about how rockets work.

cards.headline: It pushes on its own exhaust
cards.body: The Times had Level 32's law backwards. A rocket burns its propellant, and the nozzle accelerates the hot exhaust out of the back. By Newton's third law, the exhaust pushes back on the rocket, and that reaction is the thrust. Nothing outside is needed: the rocket isn't pushing on air or on the launch pad. It's pushing on its own exhaust, which works just as well in a vacuum.

cards.headline: Why a jet can't follow it up
cards.body: Burning needs an oxidizer. A jet engine takes its oxygen from the air around it, so where there's no air, it can't work. A rocket carries its oxidizer on board along with its fuel. In a liquid rocket, both are pumped into a combustion chamber, where they mix and burn. That's why a rocket works in space and a jet engine doesn't. It brings its own breath, in a sense.

cards.fact: The first liquid-fueled rocket flew for just 2.5 seconds.
cards.context: On March 16, 1926, on a farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, Goddard launched a rocket burning gasoline and liquid oxygen. It rose 41 feet and landed 184 feet away. Not a long trip, but it was the first flight of a rocket burning liquid fuel with oxygen it carried along.

title: GPS
objective: After this level you can explain how GPS satellites and precise clocks find your position.
summary: GPS receivers only listen: they time signals from at least four satellites to find distances, position and time. Satellite clocks run 38 microseconds a day fast and are corrected for relativity.

cards.headline: Your phone's GPS never sends a thing to the satellites.
cards.body: GPS satellites broadcast one-way signals, and your receiver only listens. The civilian service is free to anyone, anywhere. So how does something that just listens work out exactly where it is? It checks the time.

cards.headline: Distance from a delay
cards.body: At least 24 GPS satellites circle about 20,200 km up, each going around Earth twice a day, arranged so at least four are in view from almost anywhere. Each one broadcasts its position and the time. Your receiver notes how long each signal took to arrive. The signals travel at the speed of light, so every delay becomes a distance.

cards.headline: Why four satellites
cards.body: The satellites carry very precise atomic clocks. Your receiver's clock is far cruder, and that's a problem when timing light. So a precise fix uses four satellites: three to find the position and a fourth to correct the error in the receiver's clock. Out comes latitude, longitude, altitude and the time. Your phone gets an atomic-grade clock for free.

cards.fact: GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast.
cards.context: That's Einstein's relativity at work. Weaker gravity up there speeds the clocks by about 45 microseconds a day, and their orbital speed slows them by about 7, so engineers built in the correction. Ignore it and position errors would pile up at about 10 kilometers a day. Tiny times matter, because light travels about 300 meters in a millionth of a second.

title: Traffic
objective: After this level you can explain how traffic lights and road design keep cars moving safely.
summary: Traffic lights make crossing roads take turns, and wire loops in the road detect waiting cars by induction. Roundabouts cut conflict points from 32 to 8 and injury crashes by 72-80%.

cards.headline: The world's first traffic light exploded.
cards.body: In December 1868, a signal went up outside Parliament in London: semaphore arms by day, red and green gas lamps by night, worked by a police constable. In January 1869, a gas leak made it explode, burning the constable. Traffic control has come a long way since.

cards.headline: Red, green, and never both
cards.body: The first electric traffic signal went up in Cleveland, Ohio, on August 5, 1914: red and green lights at the corner of Euclid Avenue and East 105th Street, switched by hand from a booth. Its key design rule was that conflicting signals were impossible, so crossing roads could never both get green. That's the job of every traffic light: making drivers take turns.

cards.headline: How the light knows you're waiting
cards.body: Near many traffic lights, a loop of wire is sawn into the road. It's the most common signal sensor. An electronics unit energizes the loop with a current that keeps changing, and Level 8 showed that a changing magnetic field induces current. Park over the loop, and currents flow in your car's metal, lowering the loop's inductance. The unit reads that as a car and calls for a green.

cards.fact: A roundabout cuts 32 conflict points to 8.
cards.context: A conflict point is anywhere two drivers' paths cross, merge or split. A standard four-way intersection has 32; a single-lane roundabout has 8, and it removes the most dangerous crashes, right-angle and left-turn head-on, since everyone circles the same way. When US intersections were converted to roundabouts, injury crashes fell by 72-80%.

title: The Printing Press
objective: After this level you can explain how Gutenberg's press made books cheap and spread ideas.
summary: Gutenberg combined metal type, oil-based ink and a press. Movable type began in China and Korea, but his system took Europe from thousands of books to over 9 million by 1500.

cards.headline: Before printing, Europe had thousands of books. By 1500: over 9 million.
cards.body: Every one of those older books had been copied out by hand. Then, in only about 50 years, Europe went from thousands of books to millions. What changed was a machine, and it was really three inventions working as one.

cards.headline: Three inventions in one workshop
cards.body: Gutenberg's system had three parts. Metal type: separate letters cast from an alloy that melts easily and cools fast, tough enough to reuse. An oil-based ink, thick enough to cling to metal and print cleanly on paper. And a press, probably adapted from the ones used for wine, oil or paper, to squeeze each sheet down firmly and evenly. Set a page once, and you could print it again and again.

cards.fact: Gutenberg didn't invent movable type. He built the machine around it.
cards.context: In China, Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay in 1041-48. Korea was printing with metal type in the 14th century. Gutenberg's feat was Europe's first known mechanized printing press, which made books far cheaper to produce. Level 1's timeline puts his Bible at about 1455.

mascot.line: Luther wrote for a small debate. The printers invited everyone else.

cards.headline: When an idea outruns its author
cards.body: Martin Luther dated his 95 theses October 31, 1517. They were arguments for a scholarly debate at Wittenberg, and he didn't hand them out to the public. Others translated them into German and had them printed. Thanks to the press, they were known throughout Germany within a few weeks. Hand copying moved at the speed of a pen. Printing let an idea travel faster than the person who wrote it.

title: The Telegraph
objective: After this level you can explain how the telegraph sent messages as electric pulses.
summary: A telegraph key opens and closes a circuit; at the far end an electromagnet turns the pulses into dots and dashes. Morse's line opened in 1844, Cooke and Wheatstone's patent in 1837.

cards.headline: On May 24, 1844, a Bible verse traveled from Washington to Baltimore by wire.
cards.body: Samuel Morse tapped out "What hath God wrought!" in the Capitol, and his partner Alfred Vail read it in Baltimore. The words themselves never left Washington. So what actually traveled down the wire?

cards.headline: A switch at one end, a magnet at the other
cards.body: A telegraph is Level 4's circuit stretched between cities. The sender's key is a switch: press it and the loop closes, so current flows; let go and it opens. At the far end, that current switches an electromagnet on and off, just like the ones in Level 7. In Morse's system the magnet pulled a stylus that marked a moving strip of paper. A short signal made a dot, a longer one a dash.

mascot.line: Skip the argument over who designed it. Remember the rule: common letter, short code.

cards.headline: Morse code: the shortest mark for the commonest letter
cards.body: Dots and dashes had to spell letters, so the team gave E, the most frequent letter in English, the shortest code of all: a single dot. Less common letters got longer ones. Who designed that alphabet is still argued. Britannica credits Morse with a dot-and-dash system in 1835, but his partner Vail made many contributions, and the Franklin Institute credited Vail with the alphabet itself.

cards.fact: Britain built a telegraph too: Cooke and Wheatstone patented theirs in 1837.
cards.context: Their instrument used six wires and five needles. The current swung the needles to point at letters, the same effect that moved Ørsted's compass needle in Level 7. Two countries, two designs, one idea: a message can travel as pulses of electric current.

title: The Telephone
objective: After this level you can explain how early telephones turned voices into electric signals.
summary: A telephone turns sound into a current shaped like the sound wave, then back into sound. Bell got the 1876 patent; Gray filed the same day and Meucci earlier.

cards.headline: On one day in 1876, two inventors filed papers on the same idea.
cards.body: On February 14, 1876, Alexander Graham Bell applied for a patent on sending sound by wire. Britannica says Elisha Gray filed a caveat, a formal notice of an invention in progress, on a similar method hours later that same day, though even the order is disputed. Bell's patent came through on March 7. The argument never quite ended.

cards.headline: A current shaped like your voice
cards.body: Level 42's telegraph only switched current on and off. A telephone does something subtler. Your voice makes a thin diaphragm vibrate, and the transmitter turns those vibrations into a current that rises and falls like the sound wave itself. At the other end, the changing current drives an electromagnet that shakes a second diaphragm, rebuilding the sound. The wire carries a copy of your voice, drawn in electricity.

cards.fact: March 10, 1876: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."
cards.context: That's how Bell's lab notes record the first intelligible speech his apparatus carried. His idea leaned on Level 8's induction: a sound wave vibrating one membrane would induce a voltage in a coil, and that current could make a second, connected membrane vibrate the same way. History's first phone call was, fittingly, a request for company.

cards.headline: Who invented the telephone? It depends who you ask.
cards.body: Gray's caveat described a liquid transmitter, and Bell's March 10 success used a liquid transmitter too, one reason the fight lasted. Earlier still, Antonio Meucci had filed a caveat of his own but couldn't pay the $10 fee to keep it after 1874. In 2002 the US House of Representatives passed a resolution honoring his work on the telephone. Bell holds the patent; the credit is still argued.

title: Radio
objective: After this level you can explain how radio sends sound through the air as waves.
summary: Changing currents in antennas send and catch electromagnetic radio waves; AM or FM carries the sound. Marconi, Popov and Tesla all have claims on radio.

cards.headline: On December 12, 1901, three faint dots crossed the Atlantic with no wire.
cards.body: In Newfoundland, Guglielmo Marconi picked up the Morse letter S, sent from Cornwall. Level 42's dots had cut loose from the wire entirely. So what carried them across an ocean?

cards.headline: Radio waves are light you can't see
cards.body: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, the same family as visible light, with the longest wavelengths of all. Like light, they travel at the speed of light and need nothing to travel through, not even air. You make them with Level 9's alternating current: push a current that keeps changing up and down an antenna, and waves spread out. When they reach another antenna, they push its electrons back and forth, making a tiny matching current.

cards.headline: Riding the wave: AM and FM
cards.body: A station sends out a carrier wave at its own frequency, and tuning your radio picks that frequency out. To carry sound, the station changes the wave. AM (amplitude modulation) varies the wave's strength to match the sound. FM (frequency modulation) keeps the strength steady and varies the frequency instead. Your radio reads the changes and drives its speaker. It's Level 43's voice-shaped signal, sent through the air.

cards.fact: Who invented radio? Historians name several people.
cards.context: Heinrich Hertz first made radio waves. In Russia, Aleksandr Popov demonstrated a receiver on May 7, 1895, without knowing Marconi's work, and is hailed there as radio's inventor. Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics. And in 1943 the US Supreme Court struck down Marconi's key US tuning patent as not new, citing earlier work, chiefly John Stone Stone's, and said Tesla had anticipated several of its features.

title: Television
objective: After this level you can explain how television pictures were first sent and shown.
summary: TV scans a picture spot by spot, line by line, and rebuilds it in the same order. Baird showed mechanical TV in 1926; Farnsworth and Zworykin built electronic TV.

cards.headline: Some of the first public TV pictures had just 30 lines.
cards.body: On January 26, 1926, John Logie Baird showed his mechanical "Televisor" to members of London's Royal Institution. Mechanical TV pictures of that era had only 30 lines, repeating about 12 times a second, and they flickered badly. But they moved. How do you send a moving picture down a wire?

cards.headline: Chop the picture into lines
cards.body: You can't send a whole picture at once, but you can send it one spot at a time. A TV camera scans the scene like a reader: start at the top left, sweep right, jump back one line lower, repeat. Each spot's brightness becomes part of an electrical signal. The receiver paints the spots back in the same order, fast enough that your eye sees one whole picture rather than a racing dot.

cards.headline: Spinning disks versus electron beams
cards.body: Baird's kind of system was mechanical. It scanned with a spinning disk punched with a spiral of holes, from Paul Nipkow's 1884 patent, each hole tracing one line. Philo Farnsworth decided only electronics could scan fast enough. On September 7, 1927, his image dissector camera tube sent its first image. At the screen end, a beam of electrons swept across, and the signal set how bright each spot glowed.

cards.fact: Television has no single inventor, and its pioneers fought in court.
cards.context: Vladimir Zworykin filed for an all-electronic system in 1923, and after visiting Farnsworth's lab in 1930 he built the iconoscope camera tube at RCA. RCA fought Farnsworth's patents for years, then in 1939 agreed to pay him royalties. Baird lost out too: in February 1937 the BBC chose the electronic Marconi-EMI system over his.

title: Cameras
objective: After this level you can explain how a camera captures light, on film and on a sensor.
summary: A camera is a dark box where a lens forms an image. Film records it in silver salts; a digital sensor turns light at each pixel into an electric current.

cards.headline: The oldest surviving camera photo took hours, maybe days, to expose.
cards.body: In 1827, Nicéphore Niépce left a bitumen-coated pewter plate inside a camera obscura pointed out of his window at Le Gras. Estimates of the exposure run from about eight hours to several days. What did he need, and how do cameras do the same job now?

cards.headline: A dark box and a hole
cards.body: Camera obscura is Latin for "dark chamber." The earliest were darkened rooms with a single tiny hole. Light through the hole cast an upside-down image of the outside scene on the opposite wall. A camera is that room, shrunk: a light-tight box, a lens to focus the light, an aperture and shutter to control how much gets in, and a light-sensitive surface to catch the image.

cards.headline: Film: silver that remembers light
cards.body: Film is coated with light-sensitive silver salts, such as silver bromide. Developing turns the crystals that light struck into dark metallic silver, so bright parts of the scene come out dark: a negative. Photography's credit is shared too. Daguerre's process was announced on January 9, 1839, and Britannica says that if Talbot had announced his negative method a few weeks earlier, he would probably be called photography's founder.

cards.headline: Digital: light becomes current
cards.body: A digital camera has no film. Its sensor is covered in tiny light receptors, the pixels. When light strikes one, it induces an electric current, Level 3's moving charge, and the camera measures it and stores it as digital data. The CCD sensor was invented in 1969 by Willard Boyle and George Smith, who shared half of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

title: How a Screen Works
objective: After this level you can explain pixels and how a screen mixes red, green and blue light.
summary: A screen is a grid of pixels, about 2 million on HD. Red, green and blue light fool the eye's three cone types. An LCD passes or blocks a backlight.

cards.headline: Your screen has no yellow in it. So how does it show you a banana?
cards.body: Look closely enough at a color screen and you won't find yellow, orange or pink. Every pixel is built from just three colors: red, green and blue. The whole trick of a screen is how few colors it takes to fool your eye.

cards.headline: Pixels: pictures made of dots
cards.body: A pixel is the smallest unit of a screen image, with its own brightness and color. Millions sit in a grid, and from a normal distance your eye blends them into one smooth picture. An HD screen is 1,920 pixels across and 1,080 down: about 2 million. A 4K screen has four times as many, about 8.3 million. Level 46's camera sensor has pixels too: there they catch light, and here they give it out.

mascot.line: No yellow anywhere: your banana is red and green light, side by side.

cards.headline: Three colors fool your eye
cards.body: Your eye senses color with three types of cone cells, each most sensitive to a different range of wavelengths, roughly red, green and blue. So a screen only needs those three lights. Each pixel holds red, green and blue subpixels, and mixing light adds up: red plus green looks yellow, and all three together look white. Vary how bright each one glows, and you get a broad range of hues.

cards.headline: An LCD is a wall of tiny shutters
cards.body: An LCD makes no light of its own. A backlight shines from behind, and each subpixel has liquid crystals that change how much light gets through when a voltage is applied, behind a red, green or blue filter. Level 5's LEDs make light directly; these crystals only let it pass or block it. The screen is less a lamp than a window with millions of tiny blinds.
