title: Cell Phones
objective: After this level you can explain how cell towers pass a call from one area to the next.
summary: A cellular network splits land into cells with base stations reached by radio. Low power lets frequencies be reused, and handoff passes calls from cell to cell.

cards.headline: The first handheld cell phone call went to a rival.
cards.body: On April 3, 1973, Motorola engineer Martin Cooper used a 2.5-pound prototype to call Joel Engel of rival Bell Labs. Bell Labs had its own claim on the future: the cellular idea itself had been outlined in one of its technical memos back in 1947. So what exactly is a "cell"?

cards.headline: A cell is a patch of the map
cards.body: A cell phone is a radio, just like Level 44's. A cellular network divides the land into small areas called cells, often drawn as hexagons. Each cell has a base station, the tower your phone talks to by radio waves. The base station passes your call to a switching office, which connects it to another cell or to the ordinary phone network.

cards.headline: Why small cells mean more calls
cards.body: Phones run on batteries, so they transmit at low power and their signals don't reach far. That turns out to be the point. Because a phone's signal stays local, the frequencies used in one cell can be reused in other cells farther away. Every reuse carries another set of calls on the same airwaves. Weak signals, oddly, are what let so many people talk at once.

cards.fact: Your call can change towers mid-sentence, and you won't notice.
cards.context: As you move from one cell into the next during a call, a central controller automatically reroutes the call from the old cell's base station to the new one, without a noticeable break. This is called a handoff. On a long drive, your conversation is passed along from tower to tower like a baton in a relay race.

title: What's Inside a Smartphone
objective: After this level you can name the main parts inside a smartphone and what each one does.
summary: A smartphone joins a phone, radio, camera and screen. Its touchscreen senses a conducting finger; magnets, coils and motors make sound and buzz; lithium-ion powers it.

cards.headline: Your phone is a telephone, a radio, a camera and a screen in one case.
cards.body: Everything this chapter built fits in your pocket: Level 43's voice-to-current trick, Level 44's radio, Level 46's camera sensor and Level 47's pixels. A smartphone adds an operating system that lets you install apps. Open one up, and many of the parts are old friends.

cards.headline: The screen that feels your finger
cards.body: Most smartphones have capacitive touchscreens. The screen carries an electric field, and your finger, which conducts electricity, disturbs that field by an amount that depends on where it is. The phone works out the spot, and it can track several fingers at once. A plain plastic stylus does nothing, because plastic is an insulator, Level 4's word for a material that stops the flow of charge.

cards.headline: The speaker and the buzz
cards.body: The speaker is a coil of wire in a magnet's field. The changing current makes the coil move, the coil shakes a diaphragm, and the diaphragm pushes the air into sound, the same job as Level 43's earpiece. The buzz is a motor. Many phones spin a tiny off-center weight on a motor shaft; others, including iPhones, shake a weight on a spring with a coil. Level 7's magnets and motors, in your pocket.

cards.fact: The battery is a lithium-ion cell, a Nobel Prize-winning design.
cards.context: Lithium-ion batteries are light, rechargeable and powerful, which is why they run phones and laptops. John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing them. Level 6's rule still applies: charging drives current through the battery in reverse, running the reaction backward to store energy again. The chips that run it all get their own chapter.

title: What a Computer Is
objective: After this level you can explain input, processing, memory and output.
summary: Computer was once a job title for people who calculated. Today it means a programmable machine that takes input, processes it in a CPU, holds data in memory and sends out output.

cards.headline: In 1935, "computer" was a job title.
cards.body: That year the NACA, the agency that later became NASA, had women at its Langley lab working as computers: reading wind-tunnel data, running calculations and plotting the results. The word meant a person who computes. Today it almost always means a machine. So what does a machine need to earn the name?

mascot.line: Programmable is the word to keep. It's what lets one machine do endless jobs.

cards.fact: A computer is a programmable machine for processing, storing and displaying information.
cards.context: That's Britannica's definition, and programmable is the key word. A computer follows a set of instructions, a program, and you can swap the program. Same machine, new job. Remember Level 1: technology is knowledge put to work. A computer is a machine built to put instructions to work.

cards.headline: Four jobs: in, process, remember, out
cards.body: Every computer does four jobs. Input brings information in: a key press, a mouse click. Processing works on it, in the central processing unit, or CPU. Memory holds the data and the instructions while the work happens. Output sends the result back out, as letters on a screen or a page from the printer. Type a single letter and all four jobs take part.

cards.headline: The human computer did all four
cards.body: Picture a Langley computer at her desk. Wind-tunnel readings arrive: input. She works through the arithmetic: processing. Her notes hold the numbers in between: memory. A plotted result goes to the engineers: output. When electronic computers arrived, many of these women took on programming them. The machine didn't invent a new job. It took over a human one, and kept the job title.

title: Binary
objective: After this level you can explain how ones and zeros can stand for numbers, letters and pictures.
summary: A switch is on or off, so computers count in binary: each place is worth double and 8 bits make a byte. Letters and pixel colors are stored as numbers.

cards.headline: The words you are reading are stored as 0s and 1s.
cards.body: So are your photos and your music. A computer stores numbers, letters, colors, pictures and sounds with just two symbols. How can two symbols spell out all of that?

mascot.line: This is Level 4's switch again: closed or open, now read as 1 or 0.

cards.headline: Why only two?
cards.body: A computer is full of tiny electronic switches, and a switch has two states. Remember Level 4: a switch either closes the loop or leaves a gap. On stands for 1, off for 0. That two-symbol code is called binary ("bi" means two), and each single 0 or 1 is a bit. Everything else is built from bits.

cards.headline: Counting with doubles
cards.body: In everyday numbers each place is worth ten times the one to its right. In binary each place is worth double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. To write a number, switch on the places that add up to it. 5 is 4 + 1, so it's 101. Eight bits make a byte, running from 00000000 to 11111111: 256 patterns, for the numbers 0 to 255.

cards.headline: Letters and pictures are numbers in disguise
cards.body: Give every character a number and text becomes binary. In the ASCII code, one byte stands for one letter, digit or punctuation mark: lowercase a is 01100001. Pictures work the same way. A photo is a grid of tiny dots called pixels, and each dot's color is stored as numbers. Your favorite photo is, underneath, a very long list of numbers.

title: The Microchip
objective: After this level you can explain how transistors on a chip act as tiny switches.
summary: A transistor is a tiny semiconductor switch (Bell Labs, 1947); chips hold billions. Moore's law, an observation, saw counts double about every two years.

cards.headline: A 2020 chip holds about 7 million times the switches of a 1971 one.
cards.body: Intel's 4004 of 1971, the first commercially available microprocessor, had 2,300 transistors. Apple's M1 chip, announced in November 2020, has 16 billion. What exactly is a transistor, and how did so many squeeze onto one chip?

cards.headline: A switch with no moving parts
cards.body: A transistor is a tiny switch made from a semiconductor. No finger flips it: a small electrical signal turns it on or off, and when it's on, a larger current can flow. On is 1, off is 0, exactly Level 52's bits. John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley made the first working one at Bell Labs in December 1947.

cards.headline: Many switches, one slice of silicon
cards.body: Early transistors had to be wired together one by one. Then Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments in 1958, and Robert Noyce at Fairchild in 1959, each found a way to build many parts and the connections between them on a single piece of semiconductor, usually silicon. That's an integrated circuit: a microchip. Today's processors hold billions of transistors, switching on and off billions of times a second.

mascot.line: Despite the name, it's no law of physics. Chipmakers made it a target and kept chasing it.

cards.fact: Moore's law is an observation, not a law of nature.
cards.context: In 1965 Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, predicted the number of parts on a chip would double every year. In 1975 he revised it to every two years. Nothing in physics forces it: chipmakers turned it into a target and kept chasing it. From 2,300 to 16 billion is almost 23 doublings in 49 years, about one every two years.

summary: Software is the instructions that tell hardware what to do. Processors run only binary machine code, so compilers translate languages like Python.

cards.headline: Install an app and your phone learns a new trick. Not one part changed.
cards.body: The phone's parts are the same before and after. What changed was a set of instructions. Those instructions are software, and writing them is called coding.

cards.headline: Hardware and software
cards.body: Hardware is the physical machine: the chips, the screen, the case. Software is the instructions that tell it what to do, bundled into programs. Level 51's programmable computer is a machine that runs software. A new program doesn't change a single transistor. It changes what the transistors are told to do.

cards.headline: The processor only speaks binary
cards.body: A processor runs just one kind of instruction: machine code, written in Level 52's 0s and 1s. People find it very hard to read and write. So programmers use high-level languages such as Python or Java, which are much easier to read and write. Then something has to translate.

cards.headline: Compilers: the translators
cards.body: A compiler translates a whole program into machine code, saved to run whenever it's needed. An interpreter translates and runs it one instruction at a time instead. Grace Hopper designed one of the first compilers after joining the Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation in 1949. In 1957 her team's Flow-Matic became the first compiler for business data work written in English words.

title: Algorithms
objective: After this level you can explain algorithms as step-by-step instructions, using sorting as the example.
summary: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure with an end. In sorting, doubling the list quadruples selection sort's work but only slightly more than doubles merge sort's.

cards.headline: "Algorithm" began as a 9th-century mathematician's name.
cards.body: Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on arithmetic, and its Latin translation turned his name into Algoritmi. From that name came the word for a step-by-step way to solve a problem. That is exactly what this level is about.

cards.fact: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that solves a problem in a finite number of steps.
cards.context: Long division is one: follow the steps and you always reach the answer. In computing, a program follows an algorithm, and Level 55's code is how you hand it to the machine. The driving directions in a map app come from one. Precise steps, a definite end, a correct answer.

cards.headline: Sorting a shelf, the simple way
cards.body: Say you want a shelf of books in order by height. Selection sort: scan the whole shelf for the shortest book and move it to the front. Scan what's left for the next shortest, and repeat. It always works. But every pass rescans nearly everything, so the work grows with the square of the shelf: double the books and you roughly quadruple the scanning.

mascot.line: Same books, same shelf. The only thing that changed was the plan.

cards.headline: Sorting the clever way
cards.body: Merge sort splits the books into two halves, sorts each half the same way, then merges them: compare the front books of the two sorted piles and take the shorter, again and again. Double the books now, and the work only slightly more than doubles. Same shelf, same result, far less effort.

title: The First Computers
objective: After this level you can describe Babbage's engines, Ada Lovelace and the first electronic computers.
summary: Babbage designed mechanical computers; Lovelace wrote an early program. The ABC, Z3, Colossus and ENIAC were each first by a different rule.

cards.headline: A computer Babbage designed by 1849 was finally built in 1991.
cards.body: London's Science Museum followed Charles Babbage's plans for Difference Engine No. 2, designed in 1847-1849. The calculating section, finished in 1991, works as he intended. Babbage never saw it. So who built the first computer? That depends on your rules.

cards.headline: Babbage's Analytical Engine
cards.body: In 1834 Babbage conceived something bigger: the Analytical Engine, a mechanical machine to be programmed with punched cards. It had a store to hold numbers and a mill to do the arithmetic. Sound familiar? That's Level 51's memory and processing, sketched in brass and gears. It was never built.

cards.fact: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published what is often called the first computer program.
cards.context: Her notes on the Analytical Engine showed, step by step, how it could compute a series called the Bernoulli numbers. She also saw that it could work on letters and musical notes, not only numbers. A program for a machine that did not exist yet.

cards.headline: Four machines, four kinds of first

cards.headline: So who was first? First at what?

Even the courts got involved: in 1973 a US court ruled the ENIAC patent invalid, finding its inventors had drawn on John Atanasoff's ideas. title: Operating Systems
objective: After this level you can explain what an operating system does.
summary: An operating system shares the processor, memory and devices among programs, switching between them in tiny time slices; a start-up program loads it into RAM.

cards.headline: Music plays, a file downloads, you type a message. All at once?
cards.body: Not quite. On a single processor core, the programs take turns, switching about 50 times a second, so fast you never notice. The referee handing out those turns is the operating system.

cards.fact: An operating system is the program that manages a computer's resources for every other program.
cards.context: It shares out the processor, memory, file storage, input and output devices and network connections among the programs that need them. Windows, macOS and Linux are operating systems for computers; Android and iOS run phones. Every app you open is a guest in its house.

cards.headline: Taking turns in 20-millisecond slices
cards.body: A multitasking operating system gives each program a tiny slice of processor time, about 20 milliseconds in Windows. When the slice runs out, it pauses that program, saves its place and hands the processor to the next. That makes about 50 slices a second, so the music, the download and your typing all seem to run at once.

cards.headline: Booting: loading the boss
cards.body: Remember Level 54: RAM forgets everything when the power goes off. So each time you switch on, memory starts empty. A small start-up program stored on a chip, such as the BIOS, checks which devices are present, then loads the operating system from storage into main memory. Only then can the operating system start your apps.

title: Checkpoint: Computers

summary: One key press uses the whole chapter. The CPU loops fetch, decode, execute to a clock measured in gigahertz: billions of cycles a second.

cards.headline: Computers finale: follow one key press through the machine.
cards.body: Press the letter a. Before it shows up on your screen, nearly every idea in this chapter takes a turn. Here is the trip, and the beat that keeps it all in step.

cards.headline: One key press, start to finish
cards.body: The key press is input (Level 51). The letter becomes a byte: lowercase a is 01100001 in ASCII (Level 52). It lands in RAM (Level 54), where your app, running under the operating system, works on it. The processor's billions of transistor switches (Level 53) do the processing. The result goes out as colored pixels on your screen: output.

cards.headline: Fetch, decode, execute, repeat
cards.body: Inside the processor, one loop runs from start-up to shutdown. Fetch: the control unit pulls the next instruction from memory. Decode: it works out what the instruction means. Execute: it carries it out, often a sum or a comparison in the arithmetic-logic unit. Then it fetches the next one. Every app you've ever used is that loop, run over and over.

cards.fact: A 3.2 GHz processor's clock ticks 3.2 billion times a second.
cards.context: Clock speed counts those cycles in gigahertz: billions per second. Remember Level 9's grid, swinging back and forth 60 times a second? In one of those swings, that clock ticks about 53 million times. Speed isn't everything, though: the chip's design matters too.

title: How the Internet Began
objective: After this level you can describe ARPANET and how the internet grew from it.
summary: ARPANET, funded by the US Defense Department, sent its first message ("lo") in 1969. TCP/IP, adopted in 1983, joined separate networks into one network of networks.

cards.headline: The internet's first word was "lo."
cards.body: On October 29, 1969, a computer at UCLA tried to log in to one at the Stanford Research Institute. It sent an "l," then an "o," and then the system crashed. So how did a network that tripped over its first two letters end up connecting most of humanity?

cards.headline: A Defense Department experiment
cards.body: The network was ARPANET, funded in the late 1960s by ARPA, the research arm of the US Defense Department. It linked computers at universities and research sites. That first stuttered "lo" went from UCLA to Stanford Research Institute, and the full login worked about an hour later. By 1971 ARPANET had grown to 15 nodes. Not bad for something that crashed on its first word.

mascot.line: If you keep one thing from this level: the internet isn't a machine. It's an agreement.

cards.headline: A network of networks
cards.body: ARPANET was only one network. In 1974, Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn published TCP, a design for joining separately built networks, even radio and satellite ones, into one network of networks. On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, with every connected computer converting at the same time. That shared set of rules is what makes the internet one thing. It isn't a single machine. It's an agreement.

cards.fact: On Level 1's day clock, the internet shows up about 1.5 seconds before midnight.
cards.context: Squeeze the 3.3 million years of tools into one day, and ARPANET's 1969 "lo" lands after Edison's bulb, which arrived under 4 seconds before midnight. In that last second and a half, the internet reached about 6 billion people in 2025, roughly three-quarters of the world, according to the ITU.

title: Packets
objective: After this level you can explain how data travels in small packets that each find their own way.
summary: Packet switching chops data into small addressed packets that travel separately by any available route and are rebuilt at the end. Baran and Davies invented it independently; TCP resends lost packets.

cards.headline: Your photo never crosses the internet in one piece.
cards.body: Send a picture to a friend and it gets chopped into small pieces that travel separately, maybe by different routes, and are put back together at the other end. It sounds like a recipe for chaos. It's actually the reason the internet works.

cards.headline: Chop, label, send
cards.body: This is packet switching. A big message is broken into small packets, and each carries the address of its destination. Every packet travels independently over whatever route is available, across connected networks, and the pieces are reassembled at the end. An old phone call worked differently: it held one dedicated line for the whole conversation. Packets share the lines, like postcards from many senders riding in the same mail truck.

cards.headline: Designed to survive damage
cards.body: Why chop things up at all? In the early 1960s, Paul Baran at the RAND Corporation worked on a US Air Force network that would not fail if one of its nodes was destroyed: messages would go along whichever path still worked. In Britain, Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory reached the same idea on his own, and in a 1966 proposal he named the pieces "packets."

cards.fact: Lost packets are simply sent again.
cards.context: That's the job of the TCP half of Level 61's TCP/IP. TCP numbers the data it sends, so the receiving computer can put packets back in order and spot any gap. When a packet goes missing, it gets sent again. Think of a jigsaw puzzle with numbered pieces: you know exactly which one to ask for.

title: Undersea Cables
objective: After this level you can explain how most internet traffic crosses the oceans through cables.
summary: Over 99% of data between continents travels as laser light in glass fibers inside undersea cables. Anchors and fishing, not sharks, cause most breaks.

cards.headline: Your video call to another continent almost certainly went under the sea.
cards.body: Not up to space. Undersea cables carry over 99% of the data that travels between continents, a figure the telecom research firm TeleGeography confirmed in 2023. So what is actually lying down there on the seabed?

cards.headline: Light inside a garden hose
cards.body: Modern undersea cables are fiber-optic. Lasers at one end flash light down glass fibers about as thin as a human hair, and receivers at the far end read the flashes. The fibers are wrapped in plastic and sometimes steel wire, and across the ocean the whole cable is typically about as wide as a garden hose. In the deep sea it simply lies on the ocean floor. Near shore it's buried under the seabed and given extra armor.

mascot.line: Sharks get the blame, but anchors and fishing do the damage.

cards.fact: Ships' anchors are a bigger threat to the internet than sharks.
cards.context: Fishing vessels and dragged anchors cause about two-thirds of cable faults. Fish bites, sharks included, caused zero faults from 2007 to 2014, according to International Cable Protection Committee data. Breaks still happen, so countries use several cables and networks spread traffic across them. When one breaks, data keeps flowing over the others: Baran's idea from Level 62, a network that survives losing a piece.

cards.headline: Why not satellites?
cards.body: Satellites are great for reaching places that aren't wired yet. But cables carry far more data at a fraction of the cost. Even your phone is wireless only as far as the nearest cell tower; from there, your data rides fiber. As of 2026, TeleGeography tracks more than 600 active and planned undersea cables, a web of glass laid across the ocean floor.

summary: Wi-Fi carries data by radio across the short hop between your devices and the router; the modem links your home to the provider. The 2.4 GHz band reaches farther, the 5 GHz band is faster.

cards.headline: "Wi-Fi" doesn't stand for anything.

cards.headline: The shortest hop of the trip
cards.body: Wi-Fi uses radio waves to move data over short distances, usually less than 100 meters indoors. Your router creates the home network and passes packets to and from each device by radio. A separate box, the modem, connects that network to your internet provider. So Wi-Fi covers only the few meters from your couch to the router. Everything after that is someone else's wires.

cards.headline: Two bands: reach or speed

A hertz is one cycle per second, and giga means billion, so 2.4 GHz waves swing back and forth 2.4 billion times a second. Remember Level 9's 60-hertz AC? Wi-Fi swings 40 million times faster.

cards.fact: Your laptop and a stranger's router work together because of a 1997 rulebook.

title: The Web
objective: After this level you can explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
summary: The internet is the infrastructure; the web is one service on it, like email. Tim Berners-Lee invented the web at CERN in 1989 with HTML, URLs and HTTP, and CERN gave it away in 1993.

cards.headline: The internet is 20 years older than the web.
cards.body: ARPANET sent its first message in 1969. The World Wide Web was invented in 1989. Most people use the two words as if they meant the same thing. They don't, and the difference explains what you're actually doing every time you open a browser.

mascot.line: People mix up the internet and the web all the time. Roads and traffic: that's the difference.

cards.headline: Roads and deliveries
cards.body: The internet is the infrastructure: a huge network of computers talking to each other, the network of networks from Level 61. The web is one service built on top of it. It isn't the only one: email is another. Picture the internet as the road system and the web as one kind of traffic on it. Send an email with no browser open, and you've used the internet without touching the web.

cards.headline: Invented so scientists could share
cards.body: Tim Berners-Lee invented the web in 1989 while working at CERN, the physics lab, so scientists at universities and institutes around the world could share information automatically. By the end of 1990 he had the first web server and browser running. The server carried a handwritten label: "This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!"

cards.headline: Three ingredients, given away
cards.body: Every page still uses his three building blocks. HTML is the language a page is written in, including its hyperlinks, the clickable connections to related pages. A URL is a page's address. HTTP is the set of rules servers and browsers use to talk. Then, on April 30, 1993, CERN put the web software in the public domain, free for anyone to use. That helped the web flourish.

title: Search Engines
objective: After this level you can explain how search engines find pages and rank them.
summary: Crawlers follow links and file pages into an index, like a book's, which is what you actually search. Ranking began with links as votes (BackRub, later Google) and now weighs many signals.

cards.headline: When you search, you aren't searching the web.
cards.body: You're searching a copy. Long before you typed anything, software had already visited pages and filed what it found. When you press Enter, Google looks through that filing system, its index, not the live web. So how does the filing get done, and who decides what comes first?

cards.headline: Crawlers follow the links
cards.body: Search engines build their collections with software called crawlers. Crawlers automatically visit public web pages and follow the links on them, going from page to page much as you would when browsing. Everything they find gets organized into an index. Level 65's hyperlinks, written into each page's HTML, are the roads they travel.

cards.fact: Google's index works like the index at the back of a book.
cards.context: It has an entry for every word seen on every page it indexes, and it covers hundreds of billions of pages. Look up a word and you jump straight to the pages that contain it, with results arriving in a fraction of a second. Nobody reads the whole library; you check the index.

cards.headline: Links as votes
cards.body: But which page goes first? As Stanford graduate students, Sergey Brin and Larry Page built a search engine called BackRub that counted links. A site with thousands of links pointing at it was probably more valuable than one with a few, and a link from a heavily linked site counted as a stronger vote. BackRub grew into Google. Today ranking weighs many signals, including what your query means, how relevant and high-quality a page is, and your location.

title: The Cloud
objective: After this level you can explain what the cloud really is: computers in data centers.
summary: The cloud is shared computers in data centers, reached over the network. Data centers used about 415 billion kWh in 2024 (IEA); most becomes heat.

cards.headline: "The cloud" is a building full of computers.
cards.body: When your phone backs up its photos to the cloud, they don't float anywhere. They travel over the internet to computers in a data center, a real building that uses a lot of real electricity: about 415 billion kilowatt-hours worldwide in 2024. So what does the cloud actually do for you?

cards.headline: Renting someone else's computers
cards.body: NIST, the US standards agency, defines cloud computing as on-demand network access to a shared pool of computing resources: servers, storage, applications. You get a slice quickly when you need it and release it when you don't, with almost no setup. There is no mysterious sky machine. The cloud is someone else's computers, shared out by the slice.

title: Encryption
objective: After this level you can explain how encryption keeps messages private.
summary: Encryption uses a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext. Diffie and Hellman's 1976 public-key idea lets strangers keep secrets: one key locks, another unlocks.

cards.headline: Your messages pass through networks you'll never see.
cards.body: Remember Level 62? Your packets travel over whatever route is available, across many connected networks. So what keeps the computers along the way from reading your bank details? The packets are scrambled, and only the intended recipient can unscramble them.

cards.headline: Scramble it with a key
cards.body: Encryption uses a method and a key to turn readable plaintext into scrambled ciphertext, so only someone with the right key can read it. Julius Caesar used a simple version: he replaced each letter with the one three places down the alphabet, so HELLO became KHOOR. His key was the number three. It's also easy to crack, because there are only 25 possible shifts to try.

cards.headline: The first-secret problem
cards.body: A shared key has a catch: both sides need it before they can talk privately, and you've never met your bank's computers. How do you agree on a key when anyone might be listening? In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a blueprint for communicating over an open channel, with no prearrangement, while keeping messages secret from eavesdroppers.

cards.fact: Public-key encryption uses two keys: one locks, and a different one unlocks.
cards.context: Picture handing out open padlocks: anyone can snap one shut on a box, but only you hold the key that opens it. Public-key cryptography became the backbone of modern internet security, and it lets your browser check that your bank is really who it claims to be. The padlock icon beside a web address signals that your traffic to that site is encrypted.

title: Passwords and Hacking
objective: After this level you can explain common attacks on accounts and how to protect yours.
summary: Phishing, reused leaked passwords and guessing are common attacks. NIST and CISA advise long, unique passwords, a password manager and multifactor authentication.

cards.headline: "Password1!" follows the old rules perfectly. It's still a bad password.
cards.body: Sites that demand a capital, a number and a symbol push people toward exactly this kind of choice, notes NIST, the US standards agency, and attackers are likely to guess it. So how do accounts really get broken into, and what actually protects yours?

cards.headline: Three common ways in
cards.body: Phishing: a message with urgent language, a request for your details or a look-alike address such as amazan.com lures you to a fake page. A padlock doesn't prove a site is honest, the FBI warns; phishing sites use HTTPS too. Credential stuffing: username and password pairs leaked in one breach get tried on other sites. Guessing: attackers try common and previously leaked passwords first. None of these needs movie-style genius, just predictable habits.

cards.headline: Long beats clever
cards.body: NIST's 2025 guidance puts length first: at least 15 characters when a password is used on its own. Sites shouldn't force symbol mixes or scheduled changes, only a change after a breach. CISA suggests at least 16 characters, such as a passphrase of 4 to 7 unrelated words, and a different password for every account. A password manager makes that painless: it generates, stores and fills them in for you.

mascot.line: Long passphrase, one per account, a manager to remember them, MFA on top. That's the recipe.

cards.fact: With multifactor authentication, a stolen password alone isn't enough.
cards.context: MFA asks for two or more ways to prove it's you, such as your password plus a code or a physical security key. CISA rates security keys as the best protection against phishing and text or email codes as the weakest. Even the weakest kind means a thief needs more than your password.

title: Refrigerators
objective: After this level you can explain how a fridge moves heat out instead of making cold.
summary: A fridge moves heat out of its cold inside into the room. Refrigerant evaporates inside, soaking up heat, and condenses in outside coils. An open fridge door warms the kitchen.

cards.headline: Leave the fridge door open on a hot day, and your kitchen gets warmer.
cards.body: It sounds backwards: all that cold air spilling out. But a fridge doesn't make cold. It moves heat, and that heat has to go somewhere. Put your hand behind a running fridge and you'll feel exactly where.

mascot.line: A fridge doesn't make cold; it moves heat. Level 75 runs the same trick on a whole house.

cards.headline: A fridge is a heat mover
cards.body: Heat never flows on its own from somewhere cold to somewhere warmer. A fridge forces it to. It takes heat out of the cold box and releases it into your kitchen, which is why the area behind a running fridge feels warmer than the room. The inside gets colder because heat left, not because cold arrived. Your fridge is less a cooler than a bouncer, showing heat the door.

cards.headline: The trick: a liquid that evaporates inside
cards.body: When a liquid evaporates, it draws energy from its surroundings, and they cool down. A fridge runs a special fluid, the refrigerant, around a closed loop. It evaporates in pipes inside the fridge, soaking up heat. A compressor then squeezes the vapor, so it condenses back into liquid in coils outside the cold box and gives that heat up to the room. Then the loop starts again.

cards.fact: An open fridge door heats your kitchen.
cards.context: Level 2's rule explains it: energy is never destroyed, only changed from one form to another. With the door open, heat just circles from the room into the fridge and straight back out. Meanwhile the motor keeps running, and it adds heat of its own. The result is a warmer kitchen and a fridge working hard for nothing.

title: Microwave Ovens
objective: After this level you can explain how a microwave oven heats food.
summary: A magnetron's microwaves twist food's water molecules about 2.45 billion times a second, and the jostling is heat. Microwaves are non-ionizing and don't make food radioactive.

cards.headline: In 1945, a chocolate bar melted in an engineer's pocket.
cards.body: Percy Spencer of Raytheon had been standing near a running magnetron, a tube built for radar. Curious, he tried it on popcorn kernels, and they popped. By 1947 Raytheon had built the first microwave oven, the Radarange. So how does a radar tube cook dinner?

cards.headline: Twisting water, billions of times a second
cards.body: The magnetron fills the oven with microwaves at about 2,450 megahertz. Water molecules in food have a slightly negative oxygen end and a slightly positive hydrogen end, and like Level 3's charges, those ends get pushed and pulled. The waves' field flips about 2.45 billion times a second, twisting the molecules back and forth until they jostle their neighbors. That jostling is heat. Level 9's grid current flips 60 times a second. Microwaves are busier.

cards.headline: A metal box with a safety catch
cards.body: Microwaves bounce off metal, pass through glass, paper and plastic, and are absorbed by food. So the oven is a metal box that keeps them bouncing around inside until the food soaks them up, while your glass bowl stays out of it. And US safety rules require two separate interlocks that stop the microwaves the moment the door opens.

cards.fact: Microwaved food is not radioactive.
cards.context: Microwaves are non-ionizing radiation, like visible light and radio waves: they don't carry enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms. X-rays do, which is why they're treated with more care. In the oven, microwave energy simply turns into heat as the food absorbs it. Your leftovers come out hot, not radioactive.

title: Clean Water
objective: After this level you can explain how water is cleaned before it reaches your tap.
summary: Snow traced cholera to a pump in 1854. Plants now clump and settle dirt, filter water through sand, gravel or charcoal, and disinfect it with chlorine, which also guards the pipes.

cards.headline: In 1854, a London doctor blamed a water pump for cholera.
cards.body: Most doctors then thought disease drifted on bad air, called miasma. John Snow mapped the deaths in Soho and found them clustered around one pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle came off. Snow had shown that dirty water could kill. So how does your tap water stay clean?

cards.headline: Step one: make the dirt clump
cards.body: A treatment plant starts with coagulation: chemicals that make dirt and tiny particles stick together. Gentle stirring, called flocculation, grows them into heavier clumps called flocs. Then the water rests, and the flocs settle to the bottom, a step called sedimentation. It's a snow globe in reverse: stop shaking, and everything sinks.

cards.headline: Step two: filter, then disinfect
cards.body: Next the water runs through filters of sand, gravel or charcoal with different pore sizes, which catch leftover particles and many germs, from parasites to bacteria and viruses. Last comes disinfection: chlorine or chloramine to kill whatever germs remain. A little stays in the water on purpose, killing germs in the pipes all the way to your tap.

cards.fact: In 1908, Jersey City became the first US city to disinfect its drinking water routinely.
cards.context: Within about ten years, thousands of towns had followed. In 1900, US typhoid fever struck about 100 of every 100,000 people; by 1920 it was down to 33.8, about a third, as water treatment spread. Snow's pump handle fixed one street. Chlorine did the same job for whole cities.

title: Sewers
objective: After this level you can explain how sewers and treatment plants deal with waste water.
summary: The Great Stink of 1858 led to Bazalgette's London sewers. Modern plants let gravity bring sewage in, settle out solids, let microbes eat the rest, then disinfect it.

cards.headline: In 1858, London's river smelled so bad it disrupted Parliament.
cards.body: That hot summer, sewage baking in the River Thames produced the Great Stink, and the stench overwhelmed everyone nearby, lawmakers included. What London built next answers a question you rarely ask: where does it all go after you flush?

cards.headline: The right sewers for the wrong reason
cards.body: Parliament funded a new sewer system for all of London, overseen by the engineer Joseph Bazalgette; the city still relies on it. Officials believed disease spread through bad air, so they thought the sewers would work by removing the smell. But remember Level 73: Snow had shown that sewage in drinking water was the real killer. In 1866, London's last cholera outbreak struck parts of east London not yet connected to the new sewers. Snow was right.

cards.headline: Gravity does the first job
cards.body: Your drain feeds a sewer that mostly runs downhill, so treatment plants sit on low ground, often beside a river. First, screens catch big debris. Then the flow slows in settling tanks: heavy sludge sinks to the bottom, and floating grease and oil get skimmed off the top. So far, it's mostly patience.

cards.headline: Then the microbes get to work
cards.body: Next, air is bubbled into big tanks so microorganisms already living in the sewage can thrive. They eat much of the organic material that's left. Finally the water is disinfected with chlorine or bleach and released into a river or the ocean. The hardest-working staff at a sewage plant are too small to see.

title: Heating and Cooling
objective: After this level you can explain how heat pumps and air conditioners move heat.
summary: An air conditioner is a fridge for a house, moving heat outdoors. A heat pump runs the same trick both ways, moving about 3 kWh of heat per 1 kWh of electricity.

cards.headline: The first modern air conditioner was built for printed pages, not people.
cards.body: In 1902, engineer Willis Carrier took on a Brooklyn printing company's problem: humid air was spoiling its pages. His fix used cooling coils to control the humidity. The trick at the heart of every air conditioner since is the one inside your fridge.

mascot.line: This is Level 71's fridge again, with your house as the box.

cards.headline: An air conditioner is a fridge for your house
cards.body: Remember Level 71: a fridge moves heat out of a box and releases it into your kitchen. An air conditioner works on the same principle with a bigger box, your home. Refrigerant soaks up heat indoors and gives it up outside. In this version, your living room is the inside of the fridge, and the whole outdoors is the kitchen.

cards.headline: A heat pump runs it both ways
cards.body: A heat pump is the same kind of machine, built to work in either direction. In summer it moves heat from your home to the outdoors, like an air conditioner. In winter it flips around: it collects heat from the cool outdoor air and concentrates it inside. Even chilly air has heat to give.

cards.fact: A heat pump can move about 3 kWh of heat indoors using 1 kWh of electricity.
cards.context: An ordinary electric heater turns each kilowatt-hour, Level 10's unit, into one kilowatt-hour of heat. A heat pump spends its electricity moving heat that already exists, so it can bring in about three. Level 2's rule survives: nothing is created, just transferred. That's why heat pumps are so much more efficient than traditional heating.

title: Vaccines
objective: After this level you can explain how vaccines train the immune system.
summary: Vaccines show the immune system a harmless form of a germ so it makes antibodies and remembers. Jenner's 1796 vaccine led to smallpox's eradication. Vaccines are tested, monitored and safe.

cards.headline: Smallpox is the only human disease ever wiped out. Milkmaids helped.
cards.body: In 1796, Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox didn't catch smallpox. He turned that clue into the first successful vaccine. In 1980, after a worldwide campaign of vaccination and tracking cases, WHO declared smallpox eradicated. So how does a vaccine protect you?

cards.headline: A training exercise for your immune system
cards.body: A vaccine gives your immune system a safe preview of a germ: a killed or weakened form, a piece of one, or genetic instructions (RNA or DNA) that tell your cells to make a piece. Your immune system recognizes it, makes antibodies, which are proteins that fight disease, and remembers, all without you getting the illness. It's a fire drill without the fire.

cards.headline: Remembering is the whole point
cards.body: If the real germ turns up later, your immune system already knows it and can destroy it quickly, before you become unwell. That protection can last years, decades or even a lifetime. Instead of treating a disease after it starts, a vaccine stops you getting sick in the first place. WHO reports that over the past 50 years, vaccines against 14 diseases have saved at least 154 million lives.

cards.fact: Every vaccine is tested before use and watched after.
cards.context: Each one goes through several phases of clinical trials, involving thousands of volunteers, before it is approved. Once in use, its safety is monitored continuously. The scientific consensus, in WHO's words, is that vaccines are very safe: side effects are usually minor and brief, like a sore arm or a mild fever, and serious ones are extremely rare.

title: Seeing Inside the Body
objective: After this level you can explain how X-rays, CT scans and MRI see inside the body.
summary: Calcium-rich bone absorbs X-rays, so it shows white. CT spins an X-ray beam around you to build slices. MRI uses a magnet and radio pulses, with no ionizing radiation.

cards.headline: In 1895, a physicist photographed his wife's bones.
cards.body: Wilhelm Rontgen had just discovered X-rays, a new, penetrating kind of ray. On 22 December 1895 he made an image of his wife's hand: the bones, and a ring. Doctors quickly took up X-rays to look inside the body without surgery. Today there are several ways to see inside you, and each sees something different.

cards.headline: X-rays: a shadow picture
cards.body: X-rays carry more energy than visible light, so most of them pass straight through you. Bones, rich in calcium, absorb more of them. On the image, bones show up white, while fat, muscle and air-filled lungs appear as shades of gray. Unlike Level 72's microwaves, X-rays are ionizing radiation, which can harm living tissue, though the cancer risk from an X-ray is generally considered very small.

cards.headline: CT: X-rays from every angle
cards.body: A single X-ray squashes you into one flat shadow. A CT scanner instead spins a narrow X-ray beam around your body, and a computer turns the signals into cross-sectional slices, like a loaf of bread sliced on screen. Stack the slices, and the computer can build a 3D image.

mascot.line: X-rays and CT use ionizing radiation; MRI uses none. Keep those two groups apart.

cards.headline: MRI: a magnet and radio pulses
cards.body: An MRI reads the water inside you. Its powerful magnet lines up the protons in that water; radio pulses knock them out of line, and sensors pick up the energy they give off as they realign. It uses no ionizing radiation, and it shows soft tissue, like the brain, nerves and ligaments, more clearly than X-rays or CT. Its magnet is strong enough to fling a wheelchair across the room.

objective: After this level you can explain how antibiotics kill bacteria and why resistance matters.
summary: Penicillin (1928) stops bacteria building cell walls; antibiotics don't work on viruses. Resistant bacteria survive and multiply: about 1 in 6 infections resisted antibiotics in 2023.

cards.headline: In 1928, a moldy dish changed medicine.
cards.body: Alexander Fleming noticed that bacteria in one of his cultures wouldn't grow near a patch of Penicillium mold that had got in by accident. The mold was making penicillin. How can a drug kill bacteria and leave you alone, and why did Fleming soon worry it could stop working?

cards.headline: Break the wall, burst the germ
cards.body: Penicillin stops bacteria from building their cell walls. Without a sturdy wall, a bacterium turns leaky and fragile, and it bursts. Your own cells have no such wall, so the drug leaves them alone. That's the trick of an antibiotic: hit something bacteria have and you don't. Viruses, like those behind colds and flu, lack those targets, so antibiotics don't work on them.

mascot.line: Resistance is in the germs, not in you. That's the mix-up to avoid.

cards.headline: Resistance: the survivors win
cards.body: Antibiotic resistance doesn't mean your body gets used to a drug. It means the germs change. When an antibiotic is used, any bacteria that can defeat it survive, multiply and can even pass resistance traits in their DNA to other germs. Fleming saw it coming: in his 1945 Nobel lecture he warned that doses too small to kill microbes could make them resistant.

cards.fact: About 1 in 6 lab-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide resisted antibiotics in 2023.
cards.context: That's WHO's figure. In the US, CDC's 2019 report estimated more than 2.8 million antimicrobial-resistant infections and more than 35,000 deaths each year. WHO names the misuse and overuse of antibiotics as one of the main drivers. Every use gives resistant survivors a chance to win, which is why keeping antibiotics working matters.

title: Plastics
objective: After this level you can explain what plastic is made from and why it lasts so long.
summary: Plastics are long polymer chains, mostly from fossil-fuel carbon; Bakelite (1907) was the first fully synthetic one. Microbes can't digest them, so they break into microplastics.

cards.headline: Plastic got its start on the billiard table.
cards.body: In the 1860s, a billiards company offered a $10,000 prize for a substitute for ivory billiard balls. John Wesley Hyatt took up the challenge, and his work led to celluloid, one of the first plastics. What makes plastic so useful turns out to be what makes it so hard to get rid of.

cards.headline: Plastic is a very long chain
cards.body: Polymer means 'of many parts'. A plastic is made of long chains of small units repeated over and over, and the length of those chains makes it strong, light and flexible. Most plastics are built from carbon that comes from petroleum and other fossil fuels. In 1907, Leo Baekeland's Bakelite became the first fully synthetic plastic, made of no molecules found in nature.

cards.headline: Why nothing eats it
cards.body: Leaves and cardboard rot because microbes digest them, using enzymes to break the bonds in natural polymers such as lignin in plants. Those enzymes don't recognize the bonds that hold plastic together. So outdoors, plastic doesn't rot. It just breaks into smaller and smaller pieces, and it can take thousands of years to fully biodegrade. Being unnatural is exactly what makes it last.

cards.fact: Plastic pieces less than five millimeters long are called microplastics.
cards.context: That's about the size of a pencil eraser. Most plastic in the ocean breaks up into these small particles rather than disappearing. A bottle cap doesn't vanish; it turns into confetti.

title: Skyscrapers
objective: After this level you can explain how steel frames let buildings rise so high.
summary: Load-bearing walls thicken as buildings rise. The Home Insurance Building (1884-85) used an iron and steel skeleton instead. Tallest as of 2026: Burj Khalifa, 828 m (2010).

cards.headline: Chicago's Monadnock Building has brick walls about 2 meters thick.
cards.body: At the bottom, anyway. Its north half, finished in 1891, stands 16 stories on nothing but its own walls, and the lower walls had to be enormous to carry everything above. Build much higher that way and the ground floor turns into solid brick. So how do towers go higher?

cards.headline: When the walls do the holding up
cards.body: In a load-bearing building, the walls carry every floor above them. Each extra story adds weight to the walls below, so the tallest ones needed extremely thick walls at ground level, which ate the floor space owners wanted to rent out. The Monadnock's north half is generally regarded as the tallest office building ever held up by its walls. It is also a lesson in diminishing returns: more height, fatter walls.

mascot.line: A tablecloth doesn't hold up the table. A curtain wall doesn't hold up the building.

cards.fact: The Home Insurance Building put a skeleton inside the building.
cards.context: Chicago's 10-story Home Insurance Building (1884-85), designed by William Le Baron Jenney, is generally considered the first tall building held up by an internal iron and steel frame of columns and beams. The frame carried the floors, so the outer wall became a curtain wall: it bears only its own weight and hangs on the frame. Walls no longer had to thicken as the building rose.

cards.fact: As of 2026, the tallest building is Burj Khalifa in Dubai: 828 meters.
cards.context: That ranking comes from the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH), which keeps the official list and measures to a building's architectural top: spires count, antennas don't. Burj Khalifa has held the title since it was completed in 2010. Records like this change, so a height record always comes with a date.

title: Elevators
objective: After this level you can explain how elevators and their safety brakes made tall buildings practical.
summary: Otis's 1854 safety brake grips the guide rails if the rope fails. A counterweight means the motor lifts only the difference. Safe elevators made tall buildings practical.

cards.headline: In 1854, a man rode a platform above a New York crowd and had its rope cut.
cards.body: Elisha Otis was showing off his elevator at the Crystal Palace. The rope parted, and the platform did not fall. It was a stunt with a point: until people trusted an elevator with their lives, nobody was going to live or work very high up.

cards.headline: A brake that the fall itself switches on
cards.body: Otis's idea was a clamp held back by the rope's own pull. If the rope broke, that pull vanished, and the clamp gripped the guide rails the car runs along, holding it in place. No operator, no button: the broken rope set the brake. Modern elevators add a speed governor, which trips brakes onto the rails if the car starts down too fast.

cards.fact: An elevator's counterweight weighs about as much as the car half full.
cards.context: Car and counterweight hang from the same cables, which run over a grooved wheel called a sheave that a motor turns. As the car goes up, the counterweight goes down. So the motor only lifts the difference in weight, plus a little to beat friction. Level 2 said anything lifted high stores gravitational energy; here the two ends mostly trade it back and forth.

cards.headline: Why elevators made skyscrapers possible
cards.body: The first safe passenger elevator went into the Haughwout store in New York City in 1857. Britannica credits it with making buildings of more than four or five stories practical. Before that, stairs set the limit: nobody pays extra to haul groceries up ten flights. Pair Otis's brake with Level 81's steel frame, and the sky opens up.

title: Bridges
objective: After this level you can explain how beam, arch and suspension bridges carry their loads.
summary: Bridges resist tension and compression. Beams bend, arches push, suspension decks hang from cables. Longest span as of 2026: 2,023 m, 1915 Canakkale Bridge (2022).

cards.headline: Bend a ruler, and one face squeezes while the other stretches.
cards.body: Those are the two forces every bridge has to handle: compression, which squeezes, and tension, which stretches. Beam, arch and suspension bridges are three different answers to one question: where should the squeeze go, and where the stretch?

cards.headline: The beam: squeezed on top, stretched below
cards.body: A beam bridge is a stiff span resting on supports, like a plank over a stream. When a truck rolls on, the beam bends a little. Its top is squeezed in compression, and its bottom is stretched in tension, exactly like your ruler. So a beam needs material that can take both at once. Stand in the middle of a plank over a stream and you are running the experiment.

mascot.line: The line to keep: an arch pushes, a suspension bridge hangs.

cards.headline: Arch and suspension: push or hang
cards.body: An arch carries its load mainly by compression. Weight presses down along the curve and outward into supports at each end, which must be massive enough to hold that push. A suspension bridge flips the idea: the deck hangs from curved cables in tension. The cables pass the load to tall towers, which carry it to the ground in compression, and to anchorages at each end. An arch pushes; a suspension bridge hangs.

cards.fact: As of 2026, the longest suspension bridge span is 2,023 meters, in Turkey.
cards.context: It belongs to the 1915 Canakkale Bridge, a suspension bridge opened in 2022. It took the record from Japan's Akashi Kaikyo Bridge, which had held it since 1998, and China's Zhangjinggao Yangtze River Bridge, with a planned 2,300-meter span, is due around 2028.

title: Concrete
objective: After this level you can explain what concrete is and why both the Romans and modern builders rely on it.
summary: Concrete is sand and gravel bound by cement that hardens by reacting with water. Steel bars take the tension. A 2023 MIT-led study found lime clasts that help Roman concrete heal.

cards.headline: Concrete doesn't dry. It sets, and it can even set underwater.
cards.body: If concrete hardened the way mud does, a bridge pier poured into a river would never be ready. Instead, the cement in it reacts chemically with water. So what exactly is this stuff, and why have builders from ancient Rome to today leaned on it?

cards.headline: Artificial rock
cards.body: Concrete is sand and gravel, called aggregate, bound together by cement and water. The cement and water react (chemists call it hydration) and harden into something like artificial rock around the stones. All else being equal, less water in the mix makes stronger concrete. It is the second most-used substance in the world after water, so there is a fair chance you are standing on some right now.

mascot.line: This is Level 83's beam again: concrete takes the squeeze, steel takes the stretch.

cards.headline: Strong when squeezed, weak when stretched
cards.body: Remember Level 83's beam: squeezed on top, stretched underneath. Plain concrete handles squeezing well but copes badly with stretching, which makes it unsuitable for most structures on its own. The fix is reinforced concrete: steel bars cast inside. The steel takes the tension, the concrete takes the compression, and together they can span gaps neither could manage alone.

cards.fact: Rome's Pantheon, almost 1,900 years old, still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome.
cards.context: No steel bars at all. A 2023 MIT-led study of Roman concrete from another site, Privernum, offers one explanation for such durability: white lumps called lime clasts, formed by mixing with hot quicklime. When a crack reaches one and water gets in, dissolved calcium refills the crack as calcium carbonate. Test concrete made this way sealed its cracks within two weeks. These are findings, not a verdict on every Roman building.

title: Tunnels
objective: After this level you can explain how tunnels are dug under cities and seas.
summary: Brunel's shipworm-inspired shield dug the first tunnel under a navigable river (1843). TBMs line tunnels with concrete rings. Longest rail tunnel as of 2026: Gotthard Base, 57 km.

cards.headline: The first tunnel under a busy river was inspired by a worm.
cards.body: Around 1812, the engineer Marc Brunel saw ship's timber riddled with tunnels bored by shipworms. If those little creatures could tunnel safely, he reasoned, people could too, with the right protection. His answer shaped almost every major tunnel dug since.

cards.headline: The shield: dig at the front, line behind
cards.body: Brunel patented his tunnelling shield in 1818. Inside the iron frame, miners worked in separate cells, each digging out a small patch of the face. Then the whole shield moved forward, and masons behind it lined the fresh tunnel with brick before it could cave in. The Thames Tunnel in London, begun in 1825 and opened in 1843, became the world's first tunnel under a navigable river.

cards.headline: Today: a factory that digs
cards.body: A modern tunnel boring machine, or TBM, follows the same rule: dig at the front, line right behind. A rotating cutterhead grinds away the face, and behind it the machine fits precast concrete segments into rings, lining the tunnel as it goes. One of HS2's London machines is 198 meters long and runs around the clock as an underground factory; HS2's machines average about 16 meters a day.

cards.fact: As of 2026, the longest railway tunnel is Switzerland's Gotthard Base Tunnel: 57 km.
cards.context: It opened in 2016 and runs under the Alps, and tunnel boring machines dug most of it. Under the sea, the record is the Channel Tunnel between Britain and France, opened in 1994: about 38 km of its 50 km run beneath the seabed, the longest undersea stretch of any tunnel.

title: Steel
objective: After this level you can explain how iron becomes steel and why steel changed building.
summary: Steel is iron with up to about 2 percent carbon; cast iron has more and is brittle. Bessemer's 1856 air blast burned out carbon, made steel cheap and changed building.

cards.headline: For most of history, steel was too costly to build with.
cards.body: Then, in 1856, Henry Bessemer patented a way to turn molten iron into steel in minutes, far more cheaply than before. Steel went from special to everyday. To see why that mattered so much, start with what separates steel from plain iron.

cards.headline: Steel is iron with a pinch of carbon
cards.body: Pure iron is soft. Add carbon and it gets much harder: steel is iron with up to about 2 percent carbon. Keep going, to 2 to 4 percent, and you get cast iron, which holds up fine when squeezed but is brittle and weak when pulled. Level 83's tension is cast iron's weak spot. Steel handles pulling well, which is why it goes inside reinforced concrete.

cards.headline: Bessemer's blast
cards.body: Bessemer blew air through molten iron fresh from the furnace. The oxygen burned out the extra carbon and other impurities, and those reactions gave off so much heat that the metal stayed molten with no added fuel. Steel in minutes, with the fire feeding itself. Cheap steel soon replaced iron in railroad rails and many other uses.

cards.fact: Steel is by far the most widely used material for building the world's infrastructure.
cards.context: Britannica says cheap Bessemer steel revolutionized building construction. Level 81's Home Insurance Building caught the moment: while it was going up, rolled-steel beams were substituted for some of its iron. Railways, frames and reinforced concrete all ride on the same pinch of carbon.

title: The Assembly Line
objective: After this level you can explain how Ford's assembly line made cars cheap.
summary: In 1913 Ford moved the car past workers doing small repeated tasks. A Model T took about 90 minutes instead of over 12 hours, and its price fell from $850 to $260.

cards.headline: In 1913, Ford stopped taking workers to the car and took the car to them.
cards.body: At the Highland Park plant, a car was pulled along the floor, at first by a rope, past workers who each built their part as it arrived. The idea came from an unlikely place: a slaughterhouse.

cards.headline: Bring the work to the worker
cards.body: Slaughterhouses used a "disassembly line" to take carcasses apart step by step. Ford's engineers ran the idea in reverse. They combined three things: interchangeable parts that fit any car, work split into small tasks (each worker did one or two, over and over), and a steady flow of materials to each spot on the line. Nobody walked off to fetch a part; the car came to them.

cards.fact: A Model T went from more than 12 hours of assembly to about 90 minutes.
cards.context: Faster building made each car cheaper. Ford built over 15 million Model Ts from 1908 to 1927, and mass production let the price fall from $850 to as little as $260. Level 1's Gutenberg press pulled a similar trick for books, making them far cheaper to produce.

cards.headline: The catch: the same job all day
cards.body: Doing one or two tasks over and over was dull, and workers quit for other jobs. So in 1914 Ford made a famous offer: $5 for an eight-hour day, up from $2.34 for a nine-hour day. The line was efficient, but people still had to be persuaded to stand at it.

summary: Unimate, the first factory robot, started at General Motors in 1961. Robots are taught with a teach pendant and repeat tasks precisely; about 5 million worked in 2025.

cards.headline: The word "robot" comes from a Czech word for forced labor.
cards.body: Karel Capek used it in his 1920 play R.U.R. for manufactured workers. Forty-one years later a real one clocked in at a car plant, and its first job was handling hot metal parts.

cards.fact: The first factory robot, Unimate, started work at General Motors in 1961.
cards.context: At the plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, the one-armed Unimate lifted hot metal parts out of a die-casting machine and stacked them. It followed step-by-step commands stored on a magnetic drum and could repeat a sequence of motions again and again. George Devol invented it, and Joseph Engelberger helped build the company that sold it.

cards.headline: Teaching a robot its job
cards.body: Most factory robots don't work anything out for themselves. A trained programmer uses a handheld teach pendant to guide the arm through its task, and the robot then repeats those moves with high accuracy, shift after shift. That is why robots took dangerous or repetitive jobs first: moving materials, welding, painting, loading machines. A swinging arm can't see you, so workers are kept out of its space by barriers and sensors.

cards.fact: About 5 million industrial robots were at work in factories in 2025.
cards.context: That's the count from the International Federation of Robotics. Remember Level 87's line, where each worker did one or two tasks over and over? A robot is what that job looks like when the worker never gets bored.

title: 3D Printing
objective: After this level you can explain how 3D printers build objects layer by layer.
summary: 3D printing builds objects layer upon layer instead of cutting away. Hull's 1983 stereolithography used UV light; Crump's glue-gun frog led to FDM in 1989.

cards.headline: In 1988, a father tried to make his daughter a toy frog with a glue gun.
cards.body: Scott Crump loaded the gun with a mix of polyethylene and candle wax and built the frog up layer by layer. Then he wondered how a machine could do the same. His answer turned into one kind of 3D printer.

cards.headline: Adding, not cutting
cards.body: Most making is subtractive: you drill, cut or mill material away until the part is left, like a sculptor with a block. A 3D printer is additive. It takes a digital 3D model and builds the object layer upon layer. Nothing is carved away, which is why 3D printers are widely used to make complex components in all sorts of materials.

title: Artificial Intelligence
objective: After this level you can explain what AI is and how machine learning learns from examples.
summary: AI is a computer doing tasks we link with intelligence. Deep Blue won at chess in 1997 by brute-force speed; machine learning instead finds patterns in labeled examples, flaws and all.

cards.headline: In May 1997, a computer beat the world chess champion by sheer speed.
cards.body: IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov by brute force: it could evaluate 200 million chess positions every second. Impressive, but it's only one way to make a machine seem smart. Most of this level is about the other way, the one that learns from examples.

cards.headline: What counts as artificial intelligence
cards.body: Britannica defines AI as a computer or robot doing tasks we usually associate with intelligent beings. Beating a world champion at chess counts. The name is older than most people guess: John McCarthy coined "artificial intelligence" in 1955. And by Level 1's definition, AI is plain technology: knowledge put to work on a practical job. The job just happens to look like thinking.

cards.headline: Machine learning: rules found, not written
cards.body: Try writing down every sign of a spam email. You'll be at it a while. Machine learning flips the job around. You show a program, called a model, lots of emails already labeled "spam" or "not spam." Training tunes the model until it finds the patterns that separate them, and then it sorts new emails it has never seen. Nobody wrote those rules. The model found them in the examples.

cards.fact: A model learns what its examples teach, gaps and flaws included.
cards.context: In 2022, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) warned that biases in the data used to train AI end up in the AI itself. Models also often can't handle cases unlike the data they learned from. A spam filter trained only on English emails has simply never met a French one. Choosing the examples means choosing what the machine learns.

title: How Chatbots Work
objective: After this level you can explain in simple terms how language models predict text.
summary: A chatbot runs on a large language model that writes by predicting a likely next token, again and again. Trained on huge amounts of text, it sounds fluent but can be confidently wrong.

cards.headline: Your phone's keyboard already plays a chatbot's favorite game.
cards.body: Type "see you" and it suggests "soon." Britannica describes large language models, the engines inside chatbots, as advanced versions of that same predictive text: they aim to produce the most probable words for your prompt. So how does a guessing game write whole paragraphs, and why is it sometimes wrong?

cards.headline: One token at a time
cards.body: A language model reads and writes in tokens: small chunks of text, usually a few characters long. Given your question, it works out which token is likely to come next, adds it, and asks the same question again with the longer text. A poem, a recipe or a history essay is built this way, one small prediction after another. There's no script hidden inside. There's only "what comes next?", asked over and over.

cards.headline: Trained on mountains of text
cards.body: Where do the predictions come from? Level 91's machine learning. In training, a model works through huge amounts of text, trillions of tokens, practicing predicting what comes next. The first large language models followed a design called the transformer, introduced in 2017. Chatbots add a finishing step: when OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in November 2022, it described fine-tuning the model with human feedback so it would answer in a conversational way.

mascot.line: Sounding sure and being right are two different skills. Check the second one yourself.

cards.fact: Fluent is not the same as true.
cards.context: A model predicts the most probable words; making text sound right is not the same as checking it. So it can present something false in the same confident tone as something true, which is called a hallucination. In June 2023, a US federal judge fined two lawyers and their firm $5,000 for a brief citing six court cases that didn't exist. ChatGPT had made them up.

title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
objective: After this level you can explain how VR and AR headsets create or add to what you see.
summary: VR shows each eye a slightly different image and redraws the view as your head moves; a mismatch with your inner ear can cause motion sickness. AR adds images to the real world instead.

cards.headline: The first VR headset was so heavy it hung from the ceiling.
cards.body: In the late 1960s, Harvard's Ivan Sutherland built a head-mounted display that needed a big overhead beam to hold its weight. People jokingly called it the Sword of Damocles. Inside, you could explore a wire-frame room just by moving your head. Today's headsets are far lighter, but they pull the same two tricks.

cards.headline: Trick one: a picture for each eye
cards.body: Your two eyes see the world from slightly different spots, and your brain fuses the two views into one picture with depth. A VR headset copies that. It shows each eye its own image, offset just a little, and your brain does the rest. Lenses let your eyes focus on screens sitting only centimeters away. Two flat pictures in, one deep world out.

cards.headline: Trick two: the world follows your head
cards.body: Motion sensors track your head and redraw the view in real time, so when you turn, the virtual room turns with you. But sometimes the scene glides past while your body sits still. Your eyes report motion; your inner ear reports none. That conflict is the recipe for motion sickness, and video games and VR are known triggers for some people.

mascot.line: AR adds to your view; VR replaces it. That's the whole difference.

cards.headline: AR adds to the world instead of replacing it
cards.body: Virtual reality swaps your view for an artificial one. Augmented reality (AR) overlays computer-made images on the real scene, through a phone, glasses or a headset. You may have seen early AR without noticing: the yellow first-down line added to American football broadcasts in the mid-1990s. In 2016, Pokemon GO used a phone's camera and GPS to put cartoon creatures on real sidewalks.

title: Drones
objective: After this level you can explain how drones fly and what they are used for.
summary: A quadcopter's propellers push air down for lift; two spin each way so their twists cancel, and it steers by changing propeller speeds under a flight computer. Drones deliver blood and count birds.

cards.headline: A helicopter needs a tail rotor. A four-propeller drone doesn't.
cards.body: Spin one big rotor and the helicopter's body tries to twist the other way, so a small tail rotor pushes back. A quadcopter, the four-propeller kind of drone, has no tail at all. It hovers without spinning like a top. The secret is in which way its propellers turn.

cards.headline: Two turn one way, two turn the other
cards.body: Each propeller pushes air down, and the air pushes the drone up: action and reaction. But a spinning propeller also twists the drone's body the opposite way. So quadcopters are built with two propellers spinning clockwise and two counterclockwise. The twists cancel out, and the drone hangs steady in the air. No tail required.

cards.headline: Steering with speed alone
cards.body: A quadcopter steers with its four propellers and nothing else. Speed up the two on one side, and that side lifts; the drone tilts and slides toward the side with less lift. Speed up one spinning pair and slow the other, and the twists no longer cancel, so the drone turns on the spot. Every move is a change of speed.

cards.fact: Every quadcopter carries a tireless copilot.
cards.context: Its flight controller is an onboard computer. It reads sensors such as gyroscopes and accelerometers, compares where the drone is heading with where it should be, and adjusts the controls to hold its course. That constant correcting is what lets a machine with no rudder, no wings and no pilot aboard hang steady in the air.

cards.headline: What drones actually do
cards.body: On October 14, 2016, Rwanda launched the world's first national drone delivery service: drones built and run by the company Zipline flew blood to 21 health facilities that give transfusions. Scientists use them too: the US Geological Survey flies drones to estimate migratory bird populations and to keep watch on volcanoes. A camera that can hover turns out to be very useful.

title: Gene Editing
objective: After this level you can explain in simple terms what CRISPR gene editing does.
summary: CRISPR-Cas9, borrowed from bacteria, uses a guide RNA to find a DNA spot and Cas9 to cut it. Casgevy became the first approved CRISPR medicine in 2023; editing embryos remains widely rejected.

cards.headline: The scissors behind gene editing were borrowed from bacteria.
cards.body: Bacteria get attacked by viruses too, and they keep a memory of the attackers. They store small pieces of viral DNA in their own DNA, in patterns called CRISPR arrays. If the virus returns, they make RNA that recognizes it, and an enzyme called Cas9 cuts the virus's DNA apart. Scientists realized they could borrow the whole kit.

cards.headline: Find, cut, repair
cards.body: In 2012, Jennifer Doudna, Emmanuelle Charpentier and colleagues showed that CRISPR could edit genes. Scientists write a short guide RNA that matches the DNA they want to change. The guide leads Cas9 to that exact spot, and Cas9 cuts. Then the cell's own repair machinery takes over, and researchers use it to delete, add or change genetic material. Doudna and Charpentier shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

cards.fact: In late 2023, CRISPR became a medicine.
cards.context: In November 2023, the UK's medicines regulator authorized Casgevy, the world's first approved CRISPR therapy. On December 8, 2023, the US FDA approved it for sickle cell disease in patients 12 and older. Doctors take the patient's own blood stem cells, edit them to make more fetal hemoglobin, and return them after high-dose chemotherapy.

mascot.line: One patient, or every descendant after them. Same scissors, very different question.

cards.headline: Where to draw the line
cards.body: Casgevy edits body cells, so the change stays with one patient. Edit an egg, sperm or embryo, and the change could pass to future generations; that is illegal in the US and many other countries. In 2018, He Jiankui announced twin girls born from edited embryos, and in 2019 a Chinese court sentenced him to three years in prison. In 2023, the organizers of an international genome-editing summit, including the Royal Society, stated: "Heritable human genome editing remains unacceptable at this time."
