title: Fusion Power
objective: After this level you can explain how fusion differs from fission and why it is so hard to achieve.
summary: Fusion joins light nuclei; fission splits heavy ones. Because nuclei repel, fusion needs about 150 million °C. NIF's December 2022 shot gained energy on the target, not for the whole facility.

cards.headline: On December 5, 2022, a fusion experiment got out more than it put in.
cards.body: At the National Ignition Facility in California, 192 lasers delivered 2.05 megajoules of energy to a tiny fuel target, and fusion released 3.15 megajoules. More out than in! So why isn't fusion lighting your home? Start with what fusion is, then read the fine print.

cards.headline: Fusion joins; fission splits
cards.body: Fission releases energy by splitting heavy nuclei such as uranium. Fusion goes the other way: it joins very light nuclei into heavier ones, and it's what powers the Sun and the other stars. In the lab, the best reaction joins two kinds of hydrogen, deuterium and tritium, into helium. Fusion also can't run away: if control is lost, the reaction simply stops.

cards.headline: Why it's so hard: nuclei don't want to touch
cards.body: Remember Level 3: like charges repel. Nuclei are all positively charged, so they push each other away. To make them fuse, the fuel must be heated until the nuclei have enough energy to overcome that push. ITER says deuterium-tritium fusion needs 150,000,000 °C, 10 times hotter than the core of the Sun. At that heat the fuel is a plasma. Tokamaks hold it with magnetic fields; NIF squeezes its fuel with lasers.

mascot.line: Target gain and facility gain: two different scoreboards. Always ask which one a headline means.

cards.fact: NIF's gain was on the target, not the whole facility.
cards.context: The lasers delivered 2.05 megajoules and fusion released 3.15, a gain above 1.5 on the target. But making each shot takes about 300 megajoules of electricity from the grid, so the facility as a whole used far more energy than the fusion made. By Level 10's math, 3.15 megajoules is under one kilowatt-hour.

title: Quantum Computers
objective: After this level you can explain what makes quantum computers different, without the hype.
summary: A qubit can be 0, 1 or a mix until measured. Quantum computers are expected to help with specific jobs like simulating molecules, not replace ordinary computers; qubits are fragile and error-prone.

cards.headline: In 2019, a quantum computer did a job in 200 seconds. The argument took longer.
cards.body: Google researchers reported that their Sycamore processor finished a calculation in 200 seconds that they estimated would take a top supercomputer 10,000 years. IBM researchers replied that a better classical method could do it in 2.5 days. To judge claims like these, you need to know what a qubit is, and what it's good for.

cards.headline: A switch that isn't just on or off
cards.body: Remember Level 4's switch: open or closed, never both. An ordinary computer bit is the same, either 0 or 1. A qubit, a quantum bit, can be 0, 1 or a mix of the two, called a superposition. But the moment you measure it, you get a plain 0 or 1. The in-between only lasts until you look.

cards.headline: What they're good for
cards.body: Quantum computers aren't faster at everything. NIST expects them to help with particular problems, such as simulating the quantum rules that govern molecules, chemicals and materials. In 1994, Peter Shor described a quantum algorithm that could quickly factor the huge numbers that protect much of today's encryption. That's why, in August 2024, NIST released its first encryption standards designed to withstand quantum attacks.

mascot.line: When a headline says quantum, ask: which problem, and compared with what?

cards.headline: What they're not
cards.body: A quantum computer isn't a faster laptop: NIST sees the two kinds of machine working together, not one replacing the other. Qubits are fragile. Many must be kept near absolute zero, and today's machines make an error roughly once in every thousand operations. And that 2019 task? It was a benchmark, sampling random quantum circuits, chosen because it gets exponentially harder for ordinary computers.

title: Space Tech on Earth
objective: After this level you can name everyday technologies that came out of space research.
summary: Phone camera sensors grew from 1990s JPL research and memory foam from 1966 NASA airplane seats. Tang, Teflon and Velcro are not NASA inventions; astronauts just made them famous.

cards.headline: The camera in your phone grew out of a NASA project.
cards.body: NASA calls space technologies that end up in everyday life spinoffs, and it has published a Spinoff report every year since 1976. Some spinoffs are hiding in your pocket and under you right now. Some famous ones aren't spinoffs at all.

cards.headline: A camera on a chip
cards.body: In the 1990s, NASA wanted smaller spacecraft cameras that used less power. Eric Fossum's team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory built CMOS image sensors: a whole camera on one chip, far smaller and far thriftier with power than the sensors of the day. Small and battery-friendly turned out to be exactly what cell phones needed. Fossum called phones the killer application. The camera built for spacecraft ended up in your pocket.

cards.fact: Memory foam began as an airplane seat cushion in 1966.
cards.context: NASA's Ames Research Center wanted seats that protected people better in a crash. Charles Yost, working with NASA, made a foam that slowly molded to whatever pressed on it, then sprang back once the pressure was gone: "slow spring back foam." Later it padded football helmets, helped prevent bedsores and cushioned shoe insoles.

mascot.line: Used in space isn't the same as invented for space. That's the myth to drop.

cards.headline: Myth check: NASA didn't invent Velcro
cards.body: Some famous "space inventions" aren't. NASA itself says General Foods developed Tang in 1957, DuPont invented Teflon in 1938, and a Swiss engineer invented Velcro in the 1940s. Astronauts made them famous: John Glenn drank Tang in orbit in 1962, and Apollo missions used Velcro to anchor equipment. Using something in space isn't the same as inventing it.

title: Judging New Technology
objective: After this level you can weigh the benefits and risks of a new invention.
summary: Leaded petrol boosted engines from 1922 and harmed health until 2021. Collingridge's dilemma: effects show late, when change is hard. Ask who benefits, who bears the risk and who supplies evidence.

cards.headline: For 99 years, the world put lead in its petrol on purpose.
cards.body: From 1922, a lead compound called tetraethyllead was added to petrol to make engines run better. It worked. It also harmed people's hearts and children's developing brains. The last country stopped selling it in July 2021. How do you judge a new invention before its costs show up?

cards.headline: A benefit at the pump, a cost in the air
cards.body: The benefit was easy to see: better engine performance. The costs landed on people's health, and acting on them took decades. Most wealthy countries had banned leaded petrol by the 1980s, yet as late as 2002 almost all low- and middle-income countries still used it. The UN Environment Programme estimates that ending it prevents more than 1.2 million premature deaths a year.

cards.headline: The Collingridge dilemma
cards.body: In 1980, David Collingridge described the trap in his book The Social Control of Technology. Early on, a technology is easy to change, but nobody can yet predict its effects. By the time the effects are clear, it's everywhere and hard to change. Leaded petrol fits neatly, and the trap is worth remembering for every technology in this chapter.

mascot.line: My favorite question: who gains if I believe this? It works on headlines too.

cards.headline: Questions worth asking
cards.body: Who benefits, and who bears the risk? What's the evidence, and who supplies it? Remember Level 9: Edison, whose Pearl Street station ran on DC, claimed AC was more dangerous and electrocuted animals to prove it. Lawmakers try to match rules to risk. The European Union's AI Act, in force since August 2024, bans a few uses such as social scoring, sets strict rules for high-risk uses like hiring, and leaves minimal-risk AI such as spam filters free of new obligations.
